tripartite: The apex or portion can be trifid or tripartite.
awn inflexible: Awns can be stiff or rigid.
first order inflorescence axis pubescent hair: An inflorescence axis can be pubescent.
lateral leaf vein characteristic: PATO_0000001 is the root 'characteristic' term and too generic. The examples are mixed (straight, dichotomous, plane).
undulate: The margin can be undulate.
leaf lamina vein ascending: Veinlets can be ascending.
stem base sinuous: A stem base can be flexuose or sinuous.
drooping: A lip or lobe can be pendulous or drooping.
sharpness: An acute or acuminate apex is a valid sharpness.
lateral leaf vein parallelodromous: Parallelodromous is a venation pattern of the whole lamina. 'Lateral veins parallel' describes the relation between veins, so the bearer is wrong.
smooth: A perispore surface can be smooth.
transparent: A perispore can be hyaline (transparent).
inflorescence axis internode length: Internodes have a length.
achene fruit wrinkled: Achenes can be wrinkled.
leaf lamina vein slender: Veinlets can be slender.
pedicel quadrangular: A pedicel or peduncle can be quadrangular.
utricle capsule fruit obovate: Utricles can be obovate.
nut fruit hairy: Nuts can be hairy.
spatulate: Lobes and tips can be spatulate.
plant spore prominent: The examples describe the perispore, lobes or laesurae, not the spore. The bearer is wrong.
present: The statements say where limbidia are found, so the bearer is the limbidium and not this part.
orbicular: Calyx lobes can be orbicular.
scaphoid: Cymbiform means boat-shaped, which is scaphoid, and perianth lobes can be that shape.
vascular bundle irregular spatial pattern: The examples are about irregular areoles, a venation pattern, not the spacing of vascular bundles. The part is wrong.
capsule fruit tomentose: Capsules can be tomentose.
lodicule present: Lodicules can be present or absent.
capitulum inflorescence oblong: Capitula can be oblong.
obtuse: An apex or style branch can be obtuse.
bent: A tube can be bent.
decurrent: A base can be decurrent.
nectary cupulate: Nectaries can be cup-shaped.
raised: A palate or rim can be raised.
lodicule linear: Lodicules can be linear.
gemma spherical: Gemmae can be spherical. Some examples ('spherical clusters') describe the clusters, not the gemmae.
awn decurrent: Decurrent describes a leaf base running down the stem. The examples are moss leaves, so the pair comes from a wrong part reading, not from an awn.
present: Laesura present or absent is a normal spore character. The examples with measurements are about its length.
legume fruit winged: Winged legumes are normal, for example Pterocarpus and Dalbergia.
cotyledon fused with: Fused (connate) cotyledons are a real character.
prominent: A palate (corolla throat swelling) can be prominent. The examples are correct.
sunken: A fig ostiole can be sunken. One French example may refer to another part.
root nodule distributed: Scattered nodules on roots is a valid distribution. One example ('in the blade') is not about nodules.
root nodule punctiform: Dot-like (punctiform) nodules is a valid description of nodule shape.
whole plant tetraploid: Ploidy of the plant is meaningful. The examples are correct, including chromosome counts.
sepal abaxial epidermis sericeous: A sepal outer surface can be silky or sericeous.
areole bud increased width: Areole width is a real measurement in cacti.
anther obconical: An obconic anther is rare but real. The examples are consistent.
petal adaxial epidermis texture: The petal surface can be papillose, which is a texture. A specific papillose value would be better than the attribute.
seed optical quality: Optical quality is the wrong reading of a colour description. The examples are 'dark to pale brown' for achenes, which are fruits. Colour has its own pair.
leaf sinus decreased depth: Shallow leaf sinuses are standard.
areole bud color: Wool colour in an areole is meaningful. The wool is not named as its own part.
pappus entire: Pappus scales can have an entire margin. The examples are correct.
stem increased height: Stem height (tall) is meaningful.
capsule fruit bent: 'Angled' means angular in cross section, not bent. The PATO synonym gives a wrong reading. Use an angular or ridged shape term.
costa serrated: A serrate costa is common in mosses.
involucral bract tapered: Tapering involucral bracts are normal.
leaflet hispidulous: Hispidulous leaflets are normal.
leaf lamina sinuous: A sinuous lamina or lamina margin is a valid character. Flexuous and sinuous mean roughly the same here.
seta present: Presence of a seta (for example on teeth) is a valid statement. Some examples describe seta shape, which should get its own quality.
fruit operculum present: An operculum present or absent is a standard character. 'Anther operculate' belongs to another part.
fruit opaque: Fruits can be opaque. The examples are correct.
stolon elongated: Elongated stolons are meaningful.
pedicel floccose: A floccose pedicel is meaningful.
valve exserted: Valves can be exserted, for example in capsules.
involucral bract low saturation: A pale involucral bract is a colour statement. Low saturation is a loose reading, but it is acceptable.
oblong: Corona lobes can be oblong. Some examples are corona scales or arms, which are other parts.
vascular bundle concealed: Veins hidden or concealed is a standard leaf character. The bearer is the vascular bundle (veins).
thorn tapered: A tapered thorn is normal. Some examples ('base tapering') describe other parts.
endocarp papyraceous: A papery or chartaceous endocarp is meaningful.
present: Perichaetia present or numerous is a valid moss character. Position examples ('on terminal branches') are a different quality.
involucral bract decreased length: Short involucral bracts are meaningful. Some examples are about the petaloid portions.
filament orientation: Filament orientation (spreading, parallel) is meaningful.
pappus irregular spatial pattern: Pappus parts can be irregular. Some examples are about scale margins or length.
pappus decreased width: Narrow pappus bristles or scales are meaningful.
orbicular: A labellum lobe can be orbicular. Some examples are a callus or a different lobe.
spatulate: A corolla lip can be spatulate.
perichaetal bract length: Length of perichaetal bracts is meaningful.
flattened: Pyrenes can be flattened. The examples fit.
stamen lanate: A woolly (lanate) stamen or filament is meaningful.
branch fibrillary: The examples are 'capillary' (hair-thin), which is a shape, not fibrillary (made of small fibres).
petal introverted: Petals can be inrolled. This is a rolled margin and fits the introverted reading.
prickle terete: Terete prickles are meaningful.
flower bract coriaceous: Leathery or coriaceous bracts are meaningful.
style sericeous: A sericeous style is meaningful.
corolla velutinous: A velvety or velutinous corolla is meaningful.
tubular: A tubular ochrea is a standard character in Polygonaceae.
curvature: 'Depressed' for a stylopodium means flattened (a shape), not curvature. It should be a shape value.
lenticel oblong: Lenticels can be oblong.
sepal hispidulous: Sepals are commonly hispidulous.
septum height: Septum height is a real measurement in the examples.
papyraceous: An indusium can be papery, and the examples are correct.
concave: An orchid labellum can be concave, and the examples are correct.
sepal abaxial epidermis velutinous: The abaxial surface of a sepal can be velutinous.
banded: A spathe can be striped (banded).
recurved: The examples are about spathe throat margins, so recurved fits a spathe.
fleshy: A labellum lobe can be fleshy.
leaf sheath auricle ciliated: A leaf sheath auricle can be ciliate.
palea truncated: A palea apex can be truncate.
texture: An anther cap surface can be papillate, which is a texture.
present: Caudicles can be present or absent.
plant cell porous: Porose cells and cell walls are real (for example hyaline cells).
megasporophyll color: Colour applies to a megasporophyll (seed scale). Some examples are really indumentum colour.
lanceolate: Epicalyx segments can be lanceolate.
epicalyx ciliated: An epicalyx can be ciliate.
conspicuous: Leaf scars can be conspicuous.
prickle reflexed: Prickles can be reflexed.
capitulum inflorescence decreased length: Wrong part. 'Short-pedunculate' describes the peduncle, not the capitulum.
fruit reduced virulence: Wrong reading. 'Attenuated' was matched to 'reduced virulence', a different meaning. Attenuate is a shape.
awn terete: An awn can be terete.
laticifer cell present: Laticifer cells (lactiferous) can be present. The latex colour is a separate quality.
sepal vertical: The examples describe the 'mouth' and 'lobes' of a calyx or corolla, not the sepal. This is a wrong part.
leaflet parallelodromous: Leaflet venation can be parallel.
shoot system present: Shoots can be present or absent. 'Numerous' is a count and should go to the count pattern.
root height: 'To 4 m tall' describes the plant or a stem. Roots rarely have a height, and it was probably read as a root by mistake.
stipule semicircular: Stipules can be semicircular (semiorbicular).
stipule indurated: Stipules can become indurated.
ciliated: Labellum margins can be ciliate.
meristematic apical cell length: Apical cell length in µm is meaningful.
peristome tooth attachment quality: Peristome teeth can be united or cohering.
simple: A floral disc can be simple (single).
berry fruit pubescent hair: Berries can be pubescent. The 'glabrous' example is the opposite value.
silique fruit width: Silique width is measured.
legume fruit tomentose: A legume can be tomentellous or tomentose.
ornamented: An epichile can be ornamented with ridges or knobs.
spore capsule mouth concave: A spore capsule mouth can be concave.
texture: A disc gland surface can be verruculose, which is a texture.
prickle vestigial: Prickles can be vestigial.
bract colored: Bracts can be coloured (petaloid).
bud scale leaf entire: Bud scale margins can be entire.
root scaly: The examples describe buds, soboles and stipe bases, not roots. This is the wrong part.
leaf lamina tooth conspicuous: Leaf teeth can be conspicuous.
leaf lamina overlapping: Basal lobes of a lamina can overlap.
tepal spotted: Tepals can be spotted.

leaf lamina quality of interaction of a substance with electromagnetic radiation: Leaf lamina gloss or dullness is meaningful. It is better to use the specific values (glossy, dull) than this general PATO term.
capsule fruit rugose: A capsule surface can be rugose.
portion of secretory tissue decreased length: Wrong part. 'Glands short' or 'short-stalked' describes the gland or its stalk, not the secretory tissue.
costa ridged: A moss costa can be ridged.
perianth multi-colored: Bicoloured perianth is normal. The French examples (bicolore, coloration variée) fit.
involucral bract sinuous: Flexuous involucral bracts or bract tips are a real phyllary character, and flexuous reads as sinuous. One example is about the tips, but the bearer is the same
thorn bristly: Wrong reading. 'Bristlelike spines' describes the shape of a spine, which resembles a bristle. The thorn is not covered in bristles. Bristlelike should be a sha
calyx flared: A calyx or its limb can flare outward. The examples are correct.
involute: The margins of a corolla lip can be involute. Strictly, the margin is the bearer, but the lip carries it.
tepal present: Tepals can be present or absent, for example in distal or unisexual flowers. The examples fit.
spike inflorescence elliptic: Spikes can be elliptic in outline. The ellipsoid examples are close in meaning.
petal spoon-shaped: Spoon-shaped petals are common (spatulate or cochleariform). The examples are correct.
capsule fruit spatial pattern: Wrong reading. 'Valvate' is how the valves meet, and 'solitary or paired' is a count or arrangement of capsules. Neither is a spatial pattern of the capsule its
leaf base width: A leaf base has a measurable width. The examples are measurements.
slender: A perianth bristle (as in Cyperaceae) can be slender. The examples fit.
length: Bristle length is a standard character, given as a size or as a ratio to the achene.
petal apex notched: A petal apex can be notched or emarginate. 'Apical notch 1-3 mm' is a size of the notch, which is close enough.
bud scale leaf sericeous: Bud scales can be densely silky-hairy (sericeous). The examples are correct.
oblong: Floral corona parts (lobes, spurs, scales) are described as oblong. One example, 'horned oblong spur', is a spur of the corona, which is acceptable.
scale leaf acuminate: Scale leaves can have an acuminate apex. The English and French examples fit.
leaf lamina split: Wrong reading. 'Septate' (cross-walls in the leaf) is not 'split'. The PATO term means divided or broken, and 'not splitting when pressed' is an unrelated test.
stamen semi erect: Stamens can be suberect or erect-spreading. Some examples (connectives, spur) are other parts, but the pair is fine.
flower radiating: Wrong reading. 'Radiant' flowers (Apiaceae, Asteraceae) have enlarged outer petals or ray florets. 'Radial presentation' is symmetry. Neither means radiating in
filiform: Labellum lobes and their divisions can be filiform. The examples fit.
leaf lamina tooth ciliated: Leaf teeth can have a hair-fringed (ciliate) margin. The examples fit.
peristome tooth transparent: Hyaline means translucent, and peristome teeth in mosses can have hyaline margins or tips. Hyaline is a good fit for transparent.
pistillate flower pedicellate: A flower can be pedicellate (it has a pedicel). The French examples are about the pedicel's length and attachment, not whether it is present, but the pair is me
sporophyll dentated: Sporophylls (as in Selaginella) can have a dentate or denticulate margin. The examples fit, even though one mentions a keel.
sporophyll color: Sporophylls have a colour, for example green or yellow.
staminode entire: A staminode can have an entire margin or lobe. The examples fit.
fruit columella present: The carpophore (a fruit column in Apiaceae and Caryophyllaceae) can be present or absent. Carpophore is treated as the columella here, which is acceptable.
achene fruit laterally compressed: Achenes are commonly laterally compressed, and the negated examples are fine too.
cyme inflorescence pedunculate: Cymes can be pedunculate (stalked). The examples are correct.
resin canal amount: Resin canals are counted (2, 3-9). Counts use the amount attribute.
hairy: The gynostemium (orchid column) can be hairy. The examples describe the hairs.
leaf sheath decreased width: A leaf sheath, or its apex, can be narrow. Some examples are about the apex, but the pair is fine.
leaf sheath auricle deciduous (generic): Auricles of grass leaf sheaths are often deciduous. The examples fit.
decreased size: Vittae (oil tubes) can be small or minute. The examples fit.
color: Pinnules (the ultimate divisions of a fern frond) have a colour, for example green.
oblique orientation: Pinnules can be oblique in orientation. 'Oblique at base' is about the base shape, but the pair is meaningful.
increased thickness: Calyx lobes can be thickened, as at the apex. The examples are close enough.
triangular: The orchid labellum, its epichile and its lobes can be triangular. The French examples fit.
decreased length: The perianth tube can be short. The examples fit.
leaf lamina lobe decurrent: Leaf lobes can be decurrent. 'Base decurrent' is about the base, but the pair is meaningful.
conspicuous: A floral disc can be conspicuous or obvious. The examples fit.
pappus fibrillary: Pappus bristles are capillary (hair-fine), and fibrillary is the closest PATO term. The examples are all about the pappus.
present: False veins can be present or absent. The English and French examples fit.
triangular: Corona lobes can be triangular. The examples fit.
semicircular: The indusium (fern sorus cover) can be semicircular. The examples fit.
stem knobbled: Stems can be nodose (knobbly, with swollen nodes). The French examples fit.
ligule fringed: A grass ligule can be fringed with hairs or cilia. The examples fit.
pedicel rough: A pedicel can be rough. The examples fit.
prolate: Pseudobulbs are often ellipsoid, which is a prolate shape. If PATO has an ellipsoid term that is better, a rule should prefer it. The pair is meaningful.
plant cell inflated: Plant cells, such as moss alar cells, can be inflated. The examples fit.
leaf lamina introverted: A leaf blade, or its margins, can be inrolled. Introverted is an acceptable match.
thickness: A cupule wall has a thickness, given in mm. The examples are measurements of that wall.
oblong: The epichile (the distal part of the orchid labellum) can be oblong. The examples fit.
endocarp sculpted surface: An endocarp can be sculptured. The examples fit.
hypanthium increased width: A hypanthium or floral tube has a width, and 'wide at the throat' is a measurement of it. The pair is meaningful.
sharpness: Epicalyx segments have an acute or acuminate apex. The examples read as apex shape, but sharpness is a fair attribute for it. A rule could map acute/acuminate t
trichome knobbled: Trichomes can be nodose (knobbly, with swollen nodes). The examples are correct.
rugose: A perispore can be rugate (wrinkled or ridged). The examples are correct. Some of them describe the projections rather than the perispore.
leaf rachis flattened: Rachises and petioles are often flattened. The examples are correct.
leaf sheath strap-shaped: Wrong reading. 'Ligulate' here refers to the ligule at the sheath mouth, which is a separate part. 'Ribbonlike' alone is a weak basis. A leaf sheath is not stra
square: A floral disc, or its glands, can be roughly square. The examples are correct.
punctiform: Lithocysts or cystoliths can be punctiform (dot-like). The examples are correct.
plant cell size: Plant cells have a size, and the examples compare cells or give a size in µm.
fruit valve length: Fruit valves have a length. The examples are correct, including the 'valves 7-10 x 10-12 mm' dimension pairs.
rhizome solid configuration: Rhizomes and their internodes can be solid rather than hollow. The examples are correct.
caruncle sessile (sensu botany): A caruncle can be sessile (attached without a stalk). The examples are correct.
leaf sheath conspicuous: The examples are about the ribs of the sheath being conspicuous. The quality belongs to the ribs, not to the sheath. 'Conspicuous' is also too vague to be a use
secondary leaf vein oblique orientation: Secondary veins can be oblique to the midvein. The examples are correct.
leaf sinus length: A leaf sinus has a length or depth, often given as a fraction of the blade. The examples are correct.
endocarp blotchy: An endocarp can be blotched, as in the examples.
paraphysis orbicular: Paraphyses can be orbicular (or suborbicular) in outline. The examples are correct.
dilated: A corolla tube can be dilated or expanded at the apex. The examples are correct.
increased thickness: A corolla tube can be stout or thickened, including the thickened wall at the throat. The examples are correct.
sporangium base color: The sporangium base (apophysis) has a colour. The examples are correct.
axillary hair inconspicuous: Axillary hairs can be inconspicuous. The examples are correct.
split: Wrong reading. 'Septate' means divided by cross-walls, not split. Hyaline cells being septate is also not a quality of the cell as a whole.
pistillate flower position: A pistillate flower has a position, such as axillary. The examples are correct.
fertile lemma texture: A lemma can be rough, papillose or tuberculate. 'Pubescent' in one example is a different quality, which a rule could separate. The rest are correct.
leaflet crescent-shaped: A leaflet can be lunate (crescent-shaped). The examples are correct.
peristome dentated: A moss peristome can be toothed or dentate. The examples are correct.
pilosity: A domatium can be glabrous or hairy, so pilosity is a fair attribute. The examples are correct.
reflexed: Perianth lobes can be reflexed. The examples are correct.
aerial tuber present: 'Not bulbiferous' says that the plant bears bulbils. It does not say that the aerial tuber is present. The pair mixes up the part with what bears it. 'Aerial tu
leaf lamina banded: A leaf lamina can carry cross bands (cross-zoned, banded). The examples are correct.
leaf lamina tooth height: A leaf tooth has a height. The examples are correct.
involucral bract translucent: Involucral bracts (phyllaries) can be translucent. The examples are correct. Some of them describe the midvein or the colour (tawny-transparent).
peduncle solid configuration: A peduncle or scape can be solid rather than hollow. The examples are correct.
tuber vertical: A tuber can be vertical. The examples are correct.
disk flower fertile: A disk flower can be fertile or sterile. The examples are correct.
involucral bract decreased width: Involucral bracts can be narrow. The examples are correct.
tubular: A corona lobe can be tubular. The examples are correct.
leaf sheath clasping: A leaf sheath clasps the stem, which is the usual sense of the word. The examples are correct.
spore capsule operculum height: A moss operculum has a height. The examples are correct.
peduncle reflexed: A peduncle can be reflexed or deflexed. 'Not strongly reflexed' is a negation, which a rule handles.
portion of secretory tissue crescent-shaped: A gland (secretory tissue) can be lunate or crescent-shaped. The examples are correct.
spike inflorescence pendent: A spike can be pendent. The examples are correct.
perigynium thickness: A perigynium wall has a thickness, as in the examples.
leaf sheath firm: A leaf sheath can be firm (textured). The examples are correct.
amount: This counts epicalyx segments or bractlets. The count is a valid quality of the epicalyx segment, and the examples are correct. The counted-parts rule may cover
higher order inflorescence axis inflexible: A rachilla (a higher-order inflorescence axis) can be stiff or rigid. The examples are correct.
short shoot spheroid: Wrong part. The examples are an apex or a spur (subglobose), which belong to another part. A short shoot is not described as subglobose in them.
bracteole strap-shaped: Bracteoles can be strap-shaped or ligulate. The examples are correct.
peduncle ligneous: A peduncle can be woody (ligneous). The examples are correct.
peristome spreading: Peristome teeth spread or curve outward. The examples describe this correctly.
anther setose: Anthers can have setae at the apex or base. The examples are correct.
short shoot falciform: 'Hooked' and 'falcate' describe hairs, spines or spurs. They are not a short shoot, so this is the wrong part.
higher order inflorescence axis simple: Inflorescence branches can be simple (unbranched). The examples fit.
lamina reflexed: Laminae can reflex (bend back). The examples are correct.
branch floccose: Branches can be floccose (tufted woolly hair).
involucre lanate: Involucres are often lanate (woolly), as in Asteraceae.
thorn hard: Thorns and spines are hard. The examples fit.
plant ovary decreased width: An ovary can be narrow. Some examples refer to the apex, which is slightly off.
trichome ascending: Trichomes and hairs can be ascending.
gemma width: Gemmae are measured as length × width.
diameter: This anatomy class can have a diameter. A few examples such as '2–3 × ca. 3 cm' are not diameters.
stigma low brightness: Stigmas can be dark. 'Dark' fits low brightness.
hairy: A staminal column can be hairy.
obtuse: Apices can be obtuse. 'Rounded' is a near-synonym, so a rule may be needed to separate rounded from obtuse.
petiole decreased strength: Petioles can be weak or stiff.
shape: A cup has a shape (turbinate, goblet-shaped). The examples fit.
achene fruit keel-shaped: Achenes can be keeled. Negated examples ('not keeled') must be handled by the negation rule.
leaf lamina tip retuse: A leaf apex can be retuse (shallowly notched).
shoot axis trichome spatial pattern: 'Clathrate' (latticed) describes scales and cell walls, and 'imbriquées' is a different word. The pair comes from a wrong reading, and the part is wrong.
canal amount: Counting canals is meaningful. Some examples are grooves (sillons), which are a different part.
ligule characteristic: PATO 'characteristic' is too generic. The examples are alternatives (ciliate or fimbriate) that need specific terms.
stem obconical: A stem or caudex can be obconical.
phyllome lamina lobe obtuse: A lobe apex can be obtuse.
revolute: Margins and apices can be revolute (rolled back).
length: Disc lobes have a length. 'As long as ovary' is a comparison and needs its own handling.
tuber height: A tuber can have a height.
stem scarred: Stems carry leaf scars.
filament fusiform: Filaments can be fusiform (spindle-shaped).
height: This part can have a height.
plant ovule has fewer parts of type: 'Ovules few' counts the ovules in an ovary. It does not say the ovule has fewer parts, so it is a wrong reading. The part should be the ovary, with a count.
sessile (sensu botany): An appendix can be sessile.
spikelet ciliated: Spikelets, or their glumes, can be ciliate.
sorus oblique orientation: Sori can be oblique (they are often described this way in ferns).
convex: A disc can be convex.
secondary leaf vein distance: Veins are spaced a distance apart.
anther lanate: Anthers can be woolly or lanulose.
higher order inflorescence axis diameter: Inflorescence axes and branches have a diameter.
leaf lamina vein oblique orientation: Veins can be oblique.
banner petal diameter: A banner petal (vexillum) can have a diameter, as the examples show.
cupulate: A corona can be cup-shaped (cupular).
staminode lobed: Staminodes can be lobed.
increased width: This part can be wide.
flattened: A disc can be flattened.
flat: A crown can be flat.
spore capsule calyptra campanulate: A moss calyptra can be campanulate (bell-shaped).
plant spore decreased size: Spores are small or large. The 'lumina small' and 'minute spheres' examples describe sculpture, not the spore, so a rule is needed to ignore them.
whole plant low saturation: A pale or pallid plant is a normal colour statement for the whole plant.
staminode quadrangular: A staminode can be square or four-angled. 'Subsquare' is a fair reading.
endocarp spiny: Endocarps can be spiny. The examples mention spines, prickles and echinulate surfaces.
pedicel increased width: A pedicel can be wide or widened toward the apex.
spiny: Wrong bearer. FLOPO_0985028 is a pinnule. The examples describe the margin teeth and the apex of the pinnule, not the pinnule as a whole. These should go to the
achene fruit decreased width: An achene can be narrow. Some examples ('base narrow', 'body narrow') describe a sub-part, but the pair itself is fine.
prophyll present: Wrong reading. 'Prophyllate' says the axis or flower bears a prophyll. It does not say the prophyll itself is present. The bearer is the axis, flower or inflore
spike inflorescence spheroid: A spike can be subglobose or spheroid.
raceme inflorescence pilosity: Raceme axes and branches can be pilose, villous or glabrescent.
peristome tooth recurved: Peristome teeth are often recurved, and moss floras say so.
capsule fruit pendent: A capsule can be pendent or horizontal. That is a standard moss and fruit statement.
increased thickness: A measured value ('1.5 mm thick') belongs under the attribute thickness (PATO_0000915). It does not belong under increased thickness. This is a wrong reading, a
rhomboid: Hyaline cells in Sphagnum are described as rhombic or rhomboidal.
plant embryo terminal: An embryo can sit at the apex or terminal end of the seed or albumen. 'Embryon apical' says that.
legume fruit asymmetrical: Legumes can be asymmetric, for example at the base.
spore capsule operculum orbicular: A moss operculum (lid) can be orbicular or suborbicular.
staminate flower decreased size: Staminate flowers can be small.
lodicule subulate: Lodicules can be subulate.
secondary leaf vein concave: Secondary veins can be concave (sunken) on the upper face.
pubescent hair: An androphore (stalk of the stamens) can be pubescent. The examples describe it correctly.
thickness: A floral disc can have a measured thickness, and thickness is the right attribute for a measurement.
bracteole filamentous: Bracteoles can be filamentous.
curved: Perianth or corolla lobes can be incurved, and curved covers that.
spike inflorescence characteristic: PATO_0000001 is the root 'quality' term and says nothing. The examples are about posture (erect, drooping) or branching, which need their own terms.
perianth sessile (sensu botany): Wrong part. A perianth is not sessile. 'Perianth sessile' means the flower has no stalk, so the bearer is the flower or the pedicel.
leaf lamina tooth straight: Leaf teeth can be straight or curved.
leaf midvein low saturation: A midvein can be pale or paler than the blade.
spike inflorescence condensed: A spike can be compact or dense. 'Compressed' is a different meaning (flattened), so a rule should keep 'compact' and drop 'compressed'.
pappus width: A pappus (or its bristle bases) has a measurable width.
pappus transparent: A pappus can be hyaline, meaning translucent.
involucral bract conspicuous: Wrong part. The examples say the midnerves are evident, so the bearer is the nerve, not the bract.
involucral bract dilated: Involucral bracts can be dilated or expanded at the apex.
bract vestigial: Bracts can be rudimentary or vestigial.
leaf lamina tooth acuminate: Leaf teeth can be acuminate.
seed square: A seed can be square. The 'strophiole squarish' example is another part, so a rule should drop it.
petiole adaxial epidermis pilosity: The adaxial epidermis of a petiole can be hairy (villous, hirsute, puberulent).
hypanthium bristly: A hypanthium can be bristly.
megasporangiate strobilus shape: Seed cones have a shape, and that is the attribute term.
tubercle elongated: Tubercles can be elongate.
higher order inflorescence axis winged: An inflorescence axis (such as a rachilla) can be winged.
capsule fruit emarginate: A capsule apex can be emarginate. One example, 'not indented', is a negation, so a rule should handle it.
spore capsule operculum blunt: An operculum or its beak can be blunt.
fruit valve pubescent hair: Fruit valves can be pubescent.
size: Perianth bristles can be equal or unequal in size.
achene fruit prominent: Wrong part. The examples say the angles or ribs are prominent. The bearer is the angle or rib, not the achene.
stolon decreased length: Stolons can be short.
bract surrounding: Bracts can enclose or surround flowers or an inflorescence.
spatial pattern: Cyathia can be solitary or clustered. That is an arrangement statement.
bract obconical: Wrong part. The shape ('involucre obconic') belongs to the involucre as a whole, not to a single bract.
seed mucoid: A seed coat can be mucilaginous (mucoid).
epicalyx bract length: Epicalyx bracts have a length.
corolla flared: A corolla (throat or tube) can be flared.
hypanthium bilateral symmetry: A hypanthium can be bilaterally symmetric.
exserted: A staminal tube or column can be exserted.
leaf apex recurved: A leaf apex can be recurved.
capsule fruit semi erect: Capsules can be suberect, which is an orientation of the whole fruit.
bracteole increased size: A bracteole can be large or enlarged.
stem ciliated: Stems can be ciliate. Some examples describe margins of parts on the stem, but the pair is meaningful.
root straight: Roots and taproots can be straight.
leaf lamina lobe strap-shaped: Ligulate or strap-shaped lobes are a normal lobe shape.
length: Examples such as 'foot 3 mm long' are a measured length of the part.
sporangium increased length: 'Long-stalked' describes the stalk of the sporangium, not the length of the sporangium. This is a wrong reading, so the stalk should carry the length.
decreased size: Small lobes and small lips are meaningful.
plant embryo color: Embryo colour (white, green, yellow-brown) is a normal character.
color: The colour of bases and sheaths is meaningful.
mericarp wrinkled: Mericarps can be wrinkled.
secondary leaf vein pilosity: Leaf veins can be pubescent or glabrous, so hairiness applies.
vascular bundle sinuous: Veins are vascular bundles, and sinuous or tortuous veins are a real character. The examples mean veins, not bundles of the stem.
leaf margin introverted: Inrolled leaf margins are a standard character, and introverted fits that meaning.
sorus curved: Sori can be curved.
hypanthium thickness: Hypanthium thickness is measured, for example in fruit.
truncated: Disk glands can have a truncate apex.
size: Size of pinnules and blades, and subequal size, are meaningful.
stalk non-deciduous (any body part): Persistent stipes, meaning not shed, are meaningful.
shoot axis trichome present: The examples are about a midrib and rhizome scales, not trichomes. The part is wrong, so the pair comes from a wrong reading.
epicalyx bract shape: Epicalyx bracts have a shape.
fleshy: Disk glands can be fleshy.
bract ligneous: Bracts can be woody, and ligneous is the same thing.
attachment quality: Free versus connate lobes is a meaningful attachment character.
peristome tooth filiform: Peristome teeth can be filiform.
increased thickness: Thick or thickened walls are meaningful.
inflorescence axis internode ciliated: Rachis internodes can be ciliate.
grooved: A disc can be grooved.
capitulum inflorescence aggregated: Capitula can be clustered.
broad: A rostellum or lobe can be broad.
cladode grooved: Cladodes can be grooved.
plant ovary increased size: An ovary can be large or enlarged, for example in fruit.
ascending: Pinnae and pinnules can be ascending.
pedicel fragile: 'Delicate' here means slender or thin, not breakable. Fragile is the wrong reading, and a slenderness term should be used instead.
shoot axis internode hollow: Internodes can be hollow or fistulose.
anther brush-like shape: Anthers can be penicillate, with a tuft of hairs at the apex.
legume fruit 2-D shape: Legumes have an outline shape, such as oblong or elliptic.
lateral leaf vein spreading: Lateral veins can be patent or spreading.
shoot system terete: Shoots and stems can be terete.
semicircular: Lobes can be semicircular or semiorbicular.
size: Equal and unequal size of paired parts such as pollinia is meaningful.
anther pendent: Anthers can be pendent.
sepal adaxial epidermis sericeous: The inner surface of a sepal can be sericeous.
plant ovary hemispheroid: Ovaries can be hemispherical.
utricle capsule fruit condensed: 'Compressed' means flattened, not condensed. PATO_0001485 means something else, so this is a wrong reading.
spike inflorescence increased length: A spike can be long.
2-D shape: Disk and lobe outlines are shapes.
spatial pattern: Cupules can be solitary.
sepal floccose: Sepals can be floccose.
shoot axis internode clavate: Internodes can be clavate.
smooth: A disk or lobe can be smooth.
plant ovary dilated: An ovary can be dilated.
septum texture: A septum can be membranous, which is a texture.
cylindrical: A staminal tube is often cylindrical, and the examples show this.
fruit shriveled: Dry fruit walls shrivel or shrink, and the examples are correct.
shoot axis trichome linear: Wrong part. The examples are rhizome scales, not trichomes. A rule should send 'rhizome scale' to the scale, not to the shoot axis trichome.
slender: A caudicle (the stalk of a pollinium) can be slender.
size: Wrong part. The examples ('equal or slightly unequal', 'unequal in most leaves') are about leaves or teeth, not the vaginant lamina. Fix the bearer.
carpel prolate: Ellipsoid carpels are elongated round shapes, which is what PATO prolate means.
plant ovary bilobed: Bilobed or didymous ovaries are common, and the examples are correct.
petiole disposition: Wrong reading. 'Armed with stinging hairs' describes the hairs. The petiole is only the bearer of the hairs. Annotate it as petiole has part stinging trichome.
corolla semi erect: A suberect corolla or tube is meaningful.
anther theca size: Anther thecae can be equal or unequal in size.
achene fruit linear: Linear achenes are normal.
bract parallelodromous: Bracts can have parallel venation.
inflorescence ligneous: Woody or subligneous infructescences and catkins are meaningful.
semicircular: Calyx lobes can be semicircular (semiorbicular).
leaf trapezoid: Wrong part. The examples describe cells seen in cross section of the leaf, not the leaf. The bearer should be the cell.
non-deciduous (any body part): Indumentum can be persistent, and the examples are correct.
strobilus quadrangular: Tetragonal strobili (quadrangular in section) occur, for example in Selaginella.
plant spore bifurcated: Wrong reading. The examples are about a Y-mark sculpture on the spore surface, not a forked spore. The bearer should be the sculpture or the spore surface.
gemma inconspicuous: Gemmae can be inconspicuous.
gemma position: The position of gemmae (axillary, adaxial on the costa) is a meaningful trait in bryophytes.
pollen size: Pollen grains can be regular or irregular in size.
leaf abaxial epidermis velutinous: A velvety abaxial surface is valid, and the examples say 'abaxially' or 'below'.
plant cell sinuous: Cell walls are sinuous in many mosses and ferns.
fused with: Calyx lobes can be partly fused to each other, as the examples show.
attenuate: Corolla lobes can be attenuated, for example to the base or the apex.
corolla odor: Corollas can be scented or odourless, and the examples are correct.
ciliated: Domatia can have cilia or hair tufts.
secondary leaf vein glabrous: Secondary veins can be glabrous.
petiolule pulvinate: Petiolules can be pulvinate.
shoot axis trichome dense: Wrong part. The examples are rhizome scales, and 'densely set' describes arrangement. It is not a quality of a trichome.
spore capsule operculum heart shaped: Wrong part. 'Base cordate' describes the base of a leaf or lamina. An operculum is not described this way.
increased length: Wrong reading. The examples are plain length measurements ('9–15 mm long'), so they belong to PATO length. 'Increased length' means longer than normal.
pappus hispidulous: Pappus bristles and squamellae can be hispidulous.
portion of secretory tissue deciduous (generic): Secretory glands can be caducous, and the examples are correct.
megasporangiate strobilus cylindrical: Seed cones can be cylindrical.
megasporophyll pubescent hair: Megasporophylls (cycad scales) can be pubescent.
shape: The shape of a perianth tube is meaningful (funnelform, campanulate, cylindrical).
cauline leaf sessile (sensu botany): Cauline leaves can be sessile.
trichome translucent: Trichomes can be translucent.
exserted: Style branches can be exserted from the corolla.
seed scaphoid: Naviculate (boat-shaped) seeds are real.
dentated: Corona lobes can be toothed or dentate.
tubular: A corona or a floral tube can be tubular.
sepal mealy: Sepals can be farinose (mealy).
leaf lamina lobe fleshy: Leaf lobes can be fleshy.
filament decreased width: Narrow filaments are meaningful.
texture: The inside of a corolla tube can be papillate or scabrous.
pappus decreased size: A minute or small pappus is normal, and the examples fit.
leaf flared: A leaf blade or base can flare, and the examples fit.
root succulent: Succulent roots and taproots are common.
extrafloral nectary present: Whether an extrafloral nectary is present or absent is a normal trait. The examples mostly say 'absent', which is the opposite value, so the absent value needs
concave: The examples are about concave sides, which is a normal shape quality. The part has no label in the lexicon, so I could not check it against the part itself.
fruit increased depth: The depth in the examples belongs to the umbilicus (the fruit's basal pit), not to the whole fruit. The pair exists only through a wrong reading of the part.
inflorescence bract non-deciduous (any body part): 'Persistent' bracts are non-deciduous, which matches.
plant cell decreased width: Cells can be narrow, and the examples fit.
flower protogynous: Protogyny is a trait of the flower.
leaf lamina lobe subtriangular: Lobes can be subtriangular.
involucre inflexible: 'Rigid' means inflexible. One example is about the hairs of the involucre rather than the involucre itself, but the pair is meaningful.
root decreased width: Roots and taproots can be narrow.
filiform: Filiform lobes are a normal shape.
palea papyraceous: A chartaceous (papery) palea is normal.
leaf margin rough: A rough or scabrous margin is normal. Some examples ('coarse teeth') are really about teeth, not texture.
plant ovary bent: 'Angled' (ridged) is not 'bent'. The PATO term means something else, so the pair comes from a wrong reading.
sessile (sensu botany): A sessile lip or base is normal.
leaf sheath auricle decreased width: Auricles can be narrow.
stipule winged: Stipules can be winged or flanged. Some examples are about margins, but the quality fits.
leaf lamina lobe convex: A lobe apex or margin can be convex.
reflexed: A reflexed mid-lobe is normal.
sheath cell width: The examples are cell widths given as measurements.
flower bract ciliated: Ciliate bracts are normal.
hairy: Hairy pinnae or rachis parts are normal.
vascular bundle decreased strength: The examples are about leaf veins ('veins weak'), not vascular bundles. The part is wrong, and the veins should map to a vein class.
calyx keel-shaped: A keeled calyx is normal.
leaf lamina lobe heart shaped: Cordate lobes or lobe bases are normal.
calyx increased width: A wide or broadened calyx is normal.
stem entire: 'Entire' describes a margin, not a stem. The examples are about margins, so this is a wrong part.
coriaceous: Coriaceous (leathery) is a normal texture for leaves and similar parts.
pulvinus length: The examples are pulvinus lengths given as measurements.
leaflet ratio: A length-to-width ratio of a leaflet is normal.
pedicel inconspicuous: An inconspicuous pedicel is normal.
stigma deciduous (generic): Deciduous stigmas are normal.
keel-shaped: Keels on a part are normal.
stem node low brightness: Dark nodes are normal.
pedicel filamentous: A thread-like (filamentous) pedicel is normal.
color: The stylopodium can have a colour.
leaf lamina adaxial epidermis lanate: A lanate or woolly leaf surface is normal.
characteristic: 'Characteristic' is the root quality term and says nothing. The examples (entire or erose, ciliate) are specific states and need their own terms.
lemma increased length: A lemma can be longer than the glumes.
hairy: A hairy base or throat is normal.
inflorescence oblate: An oblate inflorescence or infructescence is meaningful.
leaflet winged: Leaflets or the rachis between them can be winged.
rhizome decreased size: A small rhizome is normal.
anther hemispheroid: Hemispherical anthers are normal, and the examples are correct.
root hard: Roots can be hard or woody. One example, 'sclerified roots', is a looser reading of the same idea.
2-D shape: The spathe limb is a blade, and the examples (ovate, oblong-ovate) are 2-D outlines.
vascular bundle depth: Wrong reading. The examples give the distance of a vein from the margin or base, which is position and not depth. The pair would need a distance or position qua
lemma tapered: A lemma apex can taper. The examples ('narrowly tapering into apex', 'lemma apex narrowed') are fine.
leaf lamina adaxial epidermis sericeous: A leaf surface can carry silky (sericeous) hairs, and the adaxial epidermis is the surface that carries them.
increased thickness: A perianth lobe can be thick or thickened. The examples are generic ('thickened', 'rather thick'), but the pair itself is sound.
leaf lamina ridged: A leaf lamina surface can be ridged. Two examples are about the midvein, which is a close but different part.
leaflet lobate: A leaflet can be lobed. 'Pinnatilobate' is a kind of lobed, but all the data come from one flora.
leaf sheath auricle linear: Auricles of the leaf sheath are described as linear, and the examples are correct.
leaf sheath banded: A sheath with stripes or bands is a valid pattern. The PATO term is 'banded', and the examples say 'stripes'.
plant ovary convex: An ovary, or its apex or face, can be convex. The examples are mostly about the apex or the adaxial side.
shoot system glistening: Shoots can be shiny.
leaf lamina tooth inflexible: Teeth can be stiff. Two examples ('rigid hairs', 'very rigid') are not about teeth, so the annotator needs to attach 'stiff' to the right noun.
leaf lamina tooth distance: The spacing between teeth is a real character, and the examples ('teeth 5-8 mm apart') are correct.
attenuate: A corolla lip can be attenuate at its base or apex.
increased size: Vittae (oil tubes) can be large or small.
inflorescence plumose: A plumose or feathery inflorescence is valid. The data come from 7 floras.
decreased size: A viscidium can be small.
keel increased length: A keel can be long. Some examples describe the claw or compare the keel with other petals, but the pair itself is valid.
keel truncated: A keel (or its base) can be truncate.
utricle capsule fruit winged: Utricles and capsules can be winged along their margins.
tertiary leaf vein present: Tertiary veins can be present or absent, and the examples are correct.
vascular bundle hard: Veins or vascular bundles can be hardened (indurate, sclerified). Some examples describe the sheaths around the bundle, so this is only moderately sure.
petal base heart shaped: A cordate petal base is a valid shape.
leaf lamina lobe branched: A leaf lobe can be forked or branched. A venation example sits in the data, but the main reading is valid.
fruit pedicel width: A fruit pedicel has a width, and the examples give width numbers.
capsule fruit symmetry: A capsule can be symmetric or asymmetric.
corolla scaphoid: Navicular (boat-shaped) parts of a corolla, such as the galea or upper lip, are valid. The examples name sub-parts, so it fits only loosely.
flower bract lanceolate: Floral bracts are often lanceolate.
portion of secretory tissue spreading: Wrong part. The examples describe glands ('glands 4, spreading') and not a portion of secretory tissue. A tissue does not spread.
gynophore decreased length: A gynophore can be short.
convex 3-D shape: A tree crown can be conical or ovoid.
linear: Rostellum arms or lobes can be linear.
convex: A pyrene can be convex on one face, such as the abaxial one.
fruit pedicel pilosity: Fruit pedicels carry hairs, such as puberulent or glabrescent.
amount: The number of stamen fascicles (phalanges) is a count.
emarginate: A calyx lobe can be emarginate at the apex.
fleshy: Calyx lobes can be fleshy.
septum width: A septum has a width, and the examples give width numbers.
tomentose: Calyx lobes can be tomentose.
winged: Corolla lobes can be winged, for example dorsally.
leaf lamina base straight: A leaf base can be straight. The data are small (only two examples).
testa present: A testa can be present or absent, and the examples show this.
stalk increased width: A stalk can be widened, for example at its base or top.
decreased size: Corona lobes (coronal scales) can be small.
leaf lamina lobe increased thickness: A leaf lobe or its margin can be thick.
megaspore spatial pattern: Megaspore ornamentation (reticulate and so on) is a spatial pattern.
hydroid present: Hydroids can be present or absent, and the examples are correct.
leaf lamina hexagonal: Wrong part. 'Hexagonal' describes the shape of laminal cells (mosses), not the lamina. It belongs to a cell bearer.
leaf hexagonal: Wrong part. 'Hexagonal' describes the shape of the cells of the leaf, not the leaf. It belongs to a cell bearer.
parenchyma present: Parenchyma can be present, and the examples ('ground tissue parenchymatous') are fine. This is a weak but acceptable use of 'present'.
native plant cell knobbled: Nodose cells or cell walls with knob-like thickenings are real, for example in mosses. The knobbled reading fits.
leaf imperforate: Aporose means having no pores, and leaves (for example Sphagnum) can lack pores on a surface. Imperforate fits.
legume fruit spherical: Globular or spherical pods are botanically meaningful, and the examples are correct.
staminode vestigial: A rudimentary staminode is a reduced, vestigial organ, so vestigial fits.
flattened: Flattened style branches are meaningful. The part is a FLOPO anatomy class with no label in the data I was given.
stem node length: The examples are 'entre-nœuds' (internodes), not nodes, so this is a wrong reading. A node has almost no length. Map internode lengths to an internode part.
cyme inflorescence width: A cyme has a width, and the examples give it.
primary leaf vein sunken: A sunken or immersed primary vein on the upper face is a standard leaf character.
pistillode width: A pistillode has dimensions. Some 'L × W' orders are ambiguous, so check that the second number is read as width.
length: Lengths in mm are meaningful for this anatomy class, and the examples are correct.
capitulum inflorescence loose: A loose or dense capitulum arrangement is meaningful. Some examples really describe the corymbs the capitula are grouped in.
leaf rachis increased thickness: A thickened rachis is meaningful, and the examples are correct.
flattened: Flattened disc glands and similar parts are meaningful.
present: The presence of an ochrea is a valid character. One example, 'veins numerous', is a wrong reading, so the item needs a check.
megasporangiate strobilus sessile (sensu botany): Sessile seed cones are meaningful, and the examples are correct.
rosette spatial pattern: Solitary or cespitose rosettes describe their spatial pattern.
petal low brightness: Dark petals or dark petal tips and veins are meaningful. Some examples are about veins and midribs, which are only parts of the petal.
seed coat reflectivity: A dull or shining seed coat is a standard character.
bulb height: Bulb dimensions are meaningful. 'Bulbs generally 2–20+' is a count, not a height, so those rows are wrong.
samara fruit shape: Samara shape (elliptic, obovate and so on) is meaningful.
involucral bract broad: Broad involucral bracts are meaningful. One example is about bract margins, a sub-part.
decreased length: A short or decreased length is meaningful for this anatomy class.
subulate: Subulate (awl-shaped) parts are meaningful, and the examples are correct.
leaf margin length: The lengths are those of cilia or of the leaf, not of the margin, which is a wrong-part reading. A margin is an edge and has no length of its own.
present: The presence of a cypsela (the fruit type) is valid.
retuse: A retuse apex is meaningful and the examples are correct.
tubercle decreased size: Minute or small tubercles are meaningful.
spike inflorescence thickness: Spike thickness in mm is meaningful and the examples are correct.
inflorescence optical quality: 'Optical quality' is too generic. The examples (pale, light green) are colour, brightness or saturation, so use those terms.
trichome sinuous: Flexuous hairs are meaningful and sinuous matches.
gynoecium glandular: A glandular gynoecium (ovary or style) is meaningful.
elaiosome length: Elaiosome length in mm is meaningful.
parenchyma mucoid: Mucilaginous parenchyma is meaningful and mucoid fits.
tepal fringed: Fringed tepals are meaningful.
thorn sparse: 'Sparse' tells how many thorns the stem or leaf bears, not a quality of one thorn. Use a count or density on the bearing part.
present: The presence of glochids is a valid character.
fruit decreased depth: The examples describe the umbilicus, the suture or the cupule, not the depth of the whole fruit. This is a wrong-part reading.
bract V-shaped: V-shaped bracts (in cross-section) are meaningful.
inflorescence bract texture: A scabrid or scabridulous bract surface is a texture character.
plant spore winged: Winged or alate spores (perispore flange) are meaningful.
fruit fragile: A fragile fruit or pericarp is meaningful.
petal base tapered: A tapered petal base is meaningful.
stem pentagonal: A pentagonal stem in cross-section is meaningful.
involucre hispidulous: A hispidulous involucre is meaningful and the examples are correct.
higher order inflorescence axis characteristic: 'Characteristic' is a PATO root term that is far too generic to annotate with. Use the specific quality, such as glandular or ascending.
leaf lamina distributed: 'Scattered' describes the hairs, scales or glands on the lamina, not the lamina itself. Use the trichome or gland as bearer.
oblong: Oblong plicae or parts are meaningful.
receptacle oblique orientation: An oblique receptacle is meaningful, as in Asteraceae.
columella sunken: An immersed or sunken columella is meaningful for mosses.
slender: A slender perianth tube or base is meaningful.
leaf lamina unbranched: The examples are about the midrib or veins being unbranched, not the lamina. This is a wrong-part reading, so use the vein or midrib as bearer.

corolla lanate: Corollas can be lanate (woolly), for example outside or in the throat. The examples are correct.
broad: A spathe can be broad. Some examples describe the inner margin, not the whole spathe, but the pair itself is meaningful.
position: Spathe position (erect, spreading, connivent) is a real character. The specific position value would be better than the general attribute.
corolla spheroid: A corolla or its tube can be subglobose or urceolate, which is a spheroid shape.
nut fruit tomentose: Nuts can be tomentose.
epicuticular wax present: A waxy bloom on a surface is a real presence character. 'Bloom' is epicuticular wax.
pilosity: A staminal tube or column can be hairy or glabrous. The examples fit.

corolla viscid: Corollas can be viscid, often through glandular hairs.
length: The length of the spathe tube is measured in the examples.
branch non-deciduous (any body part): Branches can persist or fall. 'Persistent to the trunk base' means they are not shed.
rosette aggregated: Rosettes can be clumped, which is aggregated. The negated examples ('not clumped') are still the same character.
pubescent hair: Cupules are pubescent on the inside or outside.
nut fruit sharpness: Nuts can have an acute or apiculate apex or base. The sharpness is of the nut tip, which is acceptable.
leaf lamina lobate: Leaf laminae can be lobed.
leaf lamina adaxial epidermis bristly: An epidermis can carry bristles, for example the adaxial leaf surface.
stipule elongated: Stipules can be elongate (longer than wide).
plant ovary pyramidal: An ovary can be pyramidal.
pilosity: The gynostemium (orchid column) can be hairy, bearded or villous.
sepal firm: Sepals (and keels) can be firm in texture.
involucre winged: Involucres can be winged or wingless. Only one flora so far.
lateral leaf vein spatial pattern: Lateral veins can form a reticulate pattern. A more specific reticulate term would be better, but the pair is meaningful.
samara fruit pilosity: Samaras can be pubescent, puberulent or glabrous.
short shoot circinate: 'Spur' here is the nectar spur of a flower (orchid or similar), not a short shoot. The pair exists only through the wrong part.
dissected: Pinnules of ferns and compound leaves can be dissected.
coriaceous: An indusium can be leathery (coriaceous).
glume hispid: Glumes can be hispid.
areole bud present: The examples are the areole (scar) on a nutlet, not the cactus areole bud (PO_0025353). The part is the wrong one.
pilosity: Epicalyx segments can be pilose, villous or glabrous.
secondary xylem dense: Wood (secondary xylem) is described as dense.
fleshy: Perianth lobes can be fleshy.
phyllome lamina lobe dentated: A lobe of a lamina can have a toothed margin. The statements say the margin is toothed, so the quality is carried by the lobe.
microsporophyll length: The length of a microsporophyll (cycad) is measured in the examples. Only one flora so far.
dentated: Labellum lobes or their apex or margin can be dentate.
spotted: Spathes can be spotted, for example in Araceae.
endocarp spheroid: An endocarp can be subglobose.
cylindrical: A spadix appendix can be cylindrical.
lemma spiny: Lemmas and their keels can be spinulose or spinose.
stipule ring shaped: Stipules (or the stipule scar) can be annular. Part of the evidence is the scar, not the stipule, but the pair is meaningful.
J-shaped: Fern indusia can be J-shaped. Only one flora so far.
leaf sheath auricle dentated: Leaf sheath auricles can be toothed or dentate.
subulate: Stelidia (orchid column arms) are described as subulate.
inconspicuous: Vittae can be obscure or inconspicuous.
entire: A labellum lobe margin can be entire.
short shoot broad: 'Spur' here is the flower nectar spur or its opening, not a short shoot. The pair exists only through the wrong part.
legume fruit acuminate: Legumes can have an acuminate apex.
areole bud elongated: The examples are the areole (scar) on a nutlet or similar, not the cactus areole bud. The part is the wrong one.
drupe fruit sharpness: Drupes can have an acute or apiculate apex.
present: Leaf scars can be present, prominent or conspicuous on branchlets.
fruit dissected: 'Divided into articles' means a jointed fruit (loment) that breaks into segments. It is not dissected (cut into lobes). A segmented or jointed term is needed.
cut: Pinnules or segments can be cut or incised.
sorus obtuse: 'Arrondis' means rounded (round outline), not obtuse (apex angle). The PATO term is the wrong reading. A round-shape term is needed.
scale leaf triangular: Scale leaves (cataphylls) can be triangular or deltoid.
leaf apex falciform: A leaf apex can be hooked or falcate. 'Hooked' is a close fit to falciform.
plant cell translucent: Plant cells (mainly in mosses) can be pellucid (translucent).
leaf apex present: The examples are about a hair-point, a separate structure on the apex. 'Present' belongs to the hair-point or awn, not to the leaf apex.
leaf apex filiform: A leaf apex or tip can be filiform (thread-like). The examples are correct.
leaf lamina lobe semicircular: Lobes are commonly semicircular. The examples are correct.
flower bract pilosity: Flower bracts can be hairy or glabrous. The examples (glabrescent, puberulent) are correct hair-cover states.
