oblong: A pyrene (the stone of a drupe) can be oblong. The examples are correct.
anther theca width: Anther thecae are measured in width and length. The examples are correct.
spore capsule operculum plicate: A moss operculum can be plicate. The examples are correct.
costa terete: A costa or fern rachis can be terete (round in section). The examples are correct.
truncated: An ochrea (stipular sheath) can have a truncate apex or mouth. The examples are correct.
cyme inflorescence opposite: Cymes can be opposite (arrangement on the axis). The examples are correct.
first order inflorescence axis pilosity: Inflorescence axes and rachises can be hairy or glabrous. The examples are correct.
decreased length: An androphore can be short. The examples are correct.
thallus length: A thallus is measured in length and width. The examples are correct.
alar cell decreased size: Alar cell regions can be small. The examples are correct.
alar cell well differentiated: Alar cells are described as well differentiated in mosses. The example is correct.
plant spore 2-D shape: Spore shape is a valid attribute. The examples (oval) are correct.
spore capsule calyptra inflated: A moss calyptra can be inflated around the capsule. The example is correct.
capsule fruit bilateral symmetry: A capsule can be bilaterally symmetric. The examples are correct.
petiole pulvinus increased length: The examples are plain measurements ('1–2 cm long'), which are length values, not 'increased length'. The pair comes from a wrong reading of the quality. A rule
stem imperforate: The examples are about pores in superficial cortical cells. That is a cell trait, not a stem trait, so the part is wrong. A rule should send these to the cell p
fibrillary: Sphagnum hyaline cells are fibrillose (with fibril thickenings). The examples are correct.
primary leaf vein pilosity: A primary vein can be hairy or glabrous. The examples are correct.
grooved: A rachis can be grooved (canaliculate). The examples are correct.
glandular: A rachis can bear glands below the pinna pairs, so it is glandular. The examples are correct.
legume fruit reflexed: Pods or their parts can be reflexed. The examples are correct, though the bearer may be a part of the pod.
pubescent hair: The examples describe ridges, a lateral rim and an upper part, which are not the androgynophore. The part is a wrong reading.
hairy: Style branches can be hairy, including with collecting hairs. The examples are correct.
grooved: The examples ('le haut', 'base', 'partie inférieure canaliculée') point to a petiole or stalk rather than an orchid labellum. The part is a wrong reading.
2-D shape: A connective appendage can be ovate. The examples are correct.
ray flower strap-shaped: Ray flowers are ligulate (strap-shaped). The examples are correct.
inflorescence bract scaly: Bracts can be lepidote (scaly). The examples are correct.
leaflet brochidodromous: Leaflet venation can be brochidodromous. The examples are correct.
root nodule shape: Root nodules can vary in shape (linear, elliptic, dot-like). The examples are correct.
perigynium structure: The examples (abortive, margined, jointed to the rachis) are unrelated features, not a quality of structure. This is a wrong reading, and the examples also desc
petiolule winged: A petiolule can be winged. The examples are correct.
mericarp spiny: Mericarps can be spiny. The negated examples ('without spines') need the absence rule.
capsule fruit truncated: A capsule can have a truncate apex or base. The examples are correct.
overlapping: Pinnae can overlap. The 'overlapping rachis' example is odd, but the pair is sound.
capsule fruit attachment quality: Capsules can be sessile or stipitate. The examples are correct.
rosette height: A rosette has a height or diameter. The examples are correct, though the dm size example is a mixed measurement.
involucral bract spotted: Phyllaries can be spotted. The examples are correct.
leaf lamina lobe flat: Lobes can be flat (plane). The examples are correct.
leaf lamina irregular spatial pattern: A leaf blade outline can be irregular. The examples are correct, though areolation is a different feature.
fruit solid configuration: A fruit can be solid, as opposed to hollow. The examples are correct.
perianth banded: A perianth can be striped or banded. The examples are correct.
spike inflorescence elongated: Spikes can be elongate. The examples are correct.
perigynium reflectivity: A perigynium surface can be dull or shiny. The example is correct.
color: A perigynium beak has a colour. The examples are correct.
sepal colorless: Sepals or their parts can be colourless. The examples include hairs and lobes, so the bearer may be a sepal part.
pappus element linear: Pappus scales can be linear. The examples are correct.
leaf decreased strength: The examples ('lateral veins weak') describe veins, not the leaf. The part is wrong. A rule should assign them to the vein.
flat: The FLOPO bearer is pyrene. Its faces (ventral face, sides) can be flat.
stamen fimbriated: Staminal appendages and staminodes can be fimbriate. The bearer is the stamen, which is acceptable.
bract horizontal: Bract orientation (horizontal) is meaningful, and the examples fit.
inflorescence bract elliptic: Inflorescence bracts and floral scales have elliptic outlines.
petal fragile: 'Delicate' and 'fragile' petals are a real texture, and the French 'délicats' and 'fragiles' agree.
rhizome firm: Firm is a texture, and rhizomes can be firm.
whole plant scaly: Whole plants can be scaly throughout, as in ferns and bromeliads. Use the whole plant only when the text says 'throughout'.
involucral bract sericeous: Silky or sericeous hairs are common on phyllaries.
peduncle fibrillary: Wrong reading. 'Capillary' and 'fibriform' mean hair-thin, which is filiform. PATO fibrillary means made of fibrils.
leaf blotchy: Blotched leaves are common (red or purple blotches).
bract margin transparent: Hyaline margins are translucent, so transparent fits.
achene fruit low saturation: A pale achene is a colour state, and low saturation is a near match. Prefer a 'pale' colour value if one exists.
leaf lamina abaxial epidermis rough: The abaxial epidermis can be rough, as in 'roughened abaxially'.
involucral bract lanceolate-triangular: Phyllary shape is often triangular-lanceolate.
filament lanate: Filaments can be lanate or woolly.
peduncle bristly: Peduncles can be bristly.
dentated: The bearer is the floral corona. Its margins and lobes can be dentate. Some examples describe filament margins, which is acceptable for a corona.
plant ovary circular: Ovary cross-section can be circular, though a statement should say 'in cross section'.
entire: Fronds can be entire (undivided), which is a normal fern character.
corm convex 3-D shape: A corm can be globose or subglobose. The generic parent is acceptable, but a specific spheroid term is better when one exists.
bract margin erose: Erose margins are common on bract margins.
leaf apex grooved: A canaliculate (channeled) leaf apex or acumen is grooved.
seed tessellated: A tessellate surface is a normal seed testa pattern.
catkin inflorescence width: Catkin width is a real dimension. The examples are 'length × width' pairs, so a size rule must split them.
mericarp 2-D shape: Mericarp outline shape (ovate, elliptic) is meaningful. This is the generic 2-D shape parent.
mericarp spheroid: Mericarps can be subglobose or globose.
stigma quadrangular: A stigma can be quadrate or square.
leaf midvein winged: Winged midribs are common, for example in ferns and mosses.
simple: The bearer is the pinna. A pinna can be simple (undivided), which is the opposite of compound.
leaf reduced virulence: Wrong reading. 'Attenuated' here means gradually narrowed (a shape), but PATO 'reduced virulence' has 'attenuated' as a synonym for pathogens. Map it to the tap
leaf lamina variant: A blade can be variable (variant) in size or shape. This is common in floras.
prickle broad: Prickles can be broad, and broad-based prickles are common.
prickle decreased strength: Weak prickles are a real description. This reads as strength or rigidity.
nectary spatulate: Nectary scales can be spatulate.
anther U-shaped: Anthers can be horseshoe-shaped, which is U-shaped.
present: 'Present' is not a quality of the part. The examples say where rhizophores occur (position, distribution). Presence should be handled by a rule, and the positio
perichaetal bract differentiated: Perichaetial bracts are described as differentiated or not from vegetative leaves. This is a real moss character.
higher order inflorescence axis structure: Wrong reading. 'Leafy' means bearing leaves. PATO 'structure' is a generic relational attribute and does not say this.
seed crescent-shaped: Seeds can be crescent-shaped (lunate).
decreased width: The bearer is the indusium. An indusium can be narrow.
sorus decreased length: Sori can be short.
tapered: The bearer is the pseudobulb. A pseudobulb can narrow toward its base or apex, which is tapered.
stalk filiform: Stalks, stipes and stems can be thread-like.
short shoot spreading: Wrong part. The examples describe the spur (of a flower), not a short shoot. A short shoot can spread, but these statements belong to the spur.
ovate: The bearer is the spathe. A spathe can be ovate or ovoid. This is the existing ovate-class reading.
tepal decreased size: Tepals can be small.

capitulum inflorescence has fewer parts of type: Wrong bearer. 'Capitula few' counts capitula inside a larger inflorescence, so the count belongs to the capitula (a counted part) and not to one capitulum.
erect: The bearer is the disc gland. Disc glands can be erect.
leaf apex truncated: A leaf apex can be truncate.
banded: The bearer is the orchid labellum. A labellum can be striped, though 'banded' is a loose match for stripes.
oblong: The bearer is the stigma lobe. A stigma lobe can be oblong.
pilosity: The bearer is the spathe. It can be glabrous or hairy, which is the pilosity attribute. Note that some examples describe other parts.
palea increased length: A palea can be longer than the lemma. This is a comparison, so a rule is needed to read the other part.
sepal rugose: Sepals can be rugose (wrinkled). The examples are consistent.
truncated: Spathe is the bearer (FLOPO_0986007). The apex and the throat margin of a spathe can be truncate, so the examples fit.
acuminate: Plant organ apex (FLOPO_0985023) is regularly acuminate. This is the standard apex shape.
shape: The bearer is pollinium (FLOPO_0986016). Orchid pollinia are described by shape, such as clavate, spatulate and oblanceolate.
leaf lamina mono-colored: A leaf lamina can be uniformly coloured (unicolored). The examples fit.
leaf spur shaped: Wrong reading. 'Spurred' means the base carries a spur. It does not mean the leaf is spur-shaped. Use a has-spur or has-part statement instead.
low saturation: The bearer is indusium (FLOPO_0986020). A pale or pallid indusium is a low-saturation colour. The examples fit.
pinnate: The bearer is pinnule (FLOPO_0985028). A pinnule can itself be pinnate, for example in a fern with three levels of division. Some examples describe venation on
leaf sheath oblique orientation: The mouth or apex of a grass leaf sheath can be oblique. The PATO term is imperfect, because it really describes a slanting cut, but the reading is consistent.
lemma striated: A lemma is commonly striate. The examples fit.
awn characteristic: PATO_0000001 is the root term 'quality' and says nothing. The examples are alternatives (erect or reflexed, slender or stout) and belong to specific terms such
dentated: The bearer is anther cap (FLOPO_0986034). A toothed or dentate anther cap is a genuine orchid trait.
curved: The bearer is column foot (FLOPO_0986081). An orchid column foot can be curved or upcurved.
increased height: The bearer is gynostemium or column (FLOPO_0986015). The examples are heights ('2-2.5 mm tall'), so this is a valid measurement.
leaf lamina lobe auriculate: A leaf lamina lobe can be auriculate. The examples fit.
whole plant pyramidal: A whole plant or its habit can be pyramidal. The examples fit.
rhizoid glistening: Rhizoids (in mosses) can be glossy. The examples fit.
nut fruit oblate: A nut can be oblate (flattened sphere). The examples fit.
seed coat fleshy: A seed coat can be fleshy, as in a sarcotesta. The examples fit.
caryopsis fruit shape: The shape of a caryopsis is standard. The examples fit.
fringed: The bearer is style branch (FLOPO_0986008). A style branch can be fringed with papillae or hairs.
straight: The bearer is corolla lip (FLOPO_0985017). A lip, galea or lobe can be straight. The examples fit.
length: The length of an apex is a valid measurement. Some examples are ratios to the beak, which is fine, but the bare '1.0–1.5' row has no part and should be reviewed
rhizome decreased width: A rhizome can be narrow. The examples fit.
oblique orientation: The bearer is corolla plica (FLOPO_0986067). Plicae can be oblique. The examples fit.
diameter: The bearer is stylopodium (FLOPO_0986022). Its diameter is a normal measurement in Apiaceae.
diameter: The bearer is indusium (FLOPO_0986020). Its diameter is a normal measurement in ferns.
tepal tapered: A tepal can taper. The examples fit.
hemispheroid: The bearer is tree crown (FLOPO_0985030). A crown can be hemispherical. The examples fit.
obtuse: The bearer is mentum (FLOPO_0986031). Its apex can be obtuse.
alar cell has fewer parts of type: Wrong reading. 'Alar cells few' is a count of the cells, not fewer parts of one cell. Handle it as a count of alar cells on the leaf.
short shoot prolate: Wrong part. The examples ('spur ellipsoid', 'épaississement ellipsoïdal') describe a spur or a thickening, not a short shoot. The PO term was chosen by a word m
peristome tooth fragile: A moss peristome tooth can be fragile or delicate. The examples fit.
branch mealy: A branch can have a mealy or farinose covering. The examples fit.
plant ovary scalloped: Wrong reading. The examples describe crenate ribs ('nervure crénelée') or a margin, not the ovary as a whole. The bearer should be the rib or the margin.
color: The bearer is cyathium (FLOPO_0985029). A cyathium has a colour. Check that the 'outer surface is light green' rows refer to the cyathium.
archegonium terminal: Archegonia can be terminal on the stem. The examples fit.
nectary decreased size: A nectary can be small. The examples fit.
plant ovary falciform: Wrong reading. 'Uncinate trichomes' describes hairs, not the ovary. Only the single 'ovary hooked toward apex' row is arguably the ovary.
pappus sericeous: A pappus can be sericeous or silky. The examples fit.
structure: The bearer is corolla lobe (FLOPO_0986006). PATO 'structure' is too generic. The examples (connate, free) are about fusion and should use a fused or free value
lateral leaf vein curvature: Wrong reading. 'Depressed' on the upper face means sunken or impressed veins, not curved. Use a sunken or impressed term.
portion of secretory tissue prolate: Glands can be ellipsoid. The examples fit.
follicle fruit depth: A follicle is described by three dimensions (length × width × depth or thickness). The examples are valid.
paraphysis star shaped: Paraphyses can be stellate. The examples fit.
whole plant glaucous: A whole plant can be glaucous or pruinose. The examples fit.
drupe fruit smooth: A drupe can be smooth. The examples fit.
plant cell stratification: Wrong bearer. Bistratose or unistratose counts layers of cells in a lamina, so a single cell has no stratification. The bearer should be the leaf lamina or the
loment fruit present: Wrong reading. 'Legume a loment' names the fruit type. 'Present' says nothing about a quality of the loment.
lamina oblique orientation: A lamina can have an oblique base. This is a real botanical trait, although the PATO term is imperfect.
shoot system scaly: Young shoots can be scaly. The examples fit.
stipule unstructured: Wrong reading. 'Subentire' describes the margin, a nearly smooth edge, and has nothing to do with 'unstructured'. Use the margin as the bearer with an entire va
receptacle prolate: A receptacle can be ellipsoid. The examples fit.
peristome tooth curved: Peristome teeth curve inward (incurved) in mosses. The examples are correct.
2-D shape: The bearer is the sporocarp (a fern part). Its outline seen from the side is a 2-D shape, and the examples are shapes.
mericarp attenuate: A mericarp can be narrowed gradually to its apex or base. The examples are correct.
open: The syconium ostiole (the opening of a fig) can be open or closed.
drupe fruit height: The height of a drupe is a real measurement. The examples are correct, although they sit close to length.
pilosity: A pinna rachis can be hairy (puberulent and similar). The examples are correct.
legume fruit ascending: Legume fruits (pods) can be ascending in orientation. The examples come from one flora and the plural might refer to valves or hairs, so I'm only fairly sure.
berry fruit pilosity: Berries can be hairy or glabrescent. The examples are correct.
funnel-shaped: An orchid labellum can be funnel-shaped.
scaphoid: A cymbiform or boat-shaped labellum is the same as scaphoid. This is a standard orchid term.
decreased size: A domatium can be small. The examples are correct.
ornamentation: Ornamentation is a noun for a structure, not a quality. The examples (folds, rows of papillae, a crest) are parts or textures that should be annotated for what
shoot axis trichome obtuse: The examples ('basal auricles rounded', 'apex rounded', 'base rounded') do not describe trichomes. The pair comes from the wrong part.
vascular leaf subcylindrical: Pitchers are leaves, and a pitcher can be nearly cylindrical. The examples are correct.
closed: The syconium ostiole can be closed.
plant ovary lobate: A plant ovary can be lobed (for example 6-lobed).
stipel conical: A stipel can be conical.
spike inflorescence increased width: All examples are measured widths ('5-7 mm wide'). The quality should be plain width, not 'increased width'. That is a wrong reading of the value.
calyx parallelodromous: A calyx with parallel ribs (striate-nerved) has parallel venation. The examples are correct.
xylem vessel diameter: Xylem vessels have a measurable diameter. The examples are pore diameters.
thallus spotted: A thallus can be spotted (maculate).
mericarp depth: The third number of a length × width × depth triple is the depth (thickness) of the mericarp.
achene fruit straight: An achene, or its beak, can be straight.
fruit continuous: In the examples 'continuous' describes the glands ('glands rarely continuous'), not the fruit. The pair comes from the wrong part.
leaf decreased life span: Ephemeral leaves are short-lived leaves. This matches decreased life span.
mericarp constricted: Mericarps can be constricted (between the seeds). The examples are correct.
length: The length of an epicalyx segment, here stated relative to the sepals, is a valid quality.
palea spatulate: A palea can be spatulate.
achene fruit plumose: Achenes with a feathery beak or pappus are called plumose. The examples are correct.
petal cream: Petals can be cream-coloured.
stem cane-like: Stems can be cane-like or wand-like.
tepal abaxial epidermis color: The colour of the outer (abaxial) side of a tepal is valid.
warty: A corolla lip can be warty (verrucose).
awn spiny: An awn can be spinulose, meaning it has small spines.
capsule fruit acuminate: A capsule, or its apex, can be acuminate.
present: A rostellum (an orchid part) can be present or absent.
leaf sheath U-shaped: The summit (mouth) of a leaf sheath can be U-shaped.
leaf sheath fibrillary: Old leaf sheaths can be fibrillose, with fine fibres.
spike inflorescence semi erect: Spikes can be suberect, meaning nearly erect.
leaf margin decreased width: A leaf margin or border can be narrow.
short shoot erect: Short shoots can be erect. Some examples are about spurs, but they are the same kind of part.
pilosity: A pinnule can be hairy or glabrous, including on one side only.
branch decreased strength: Branches can be weak. The examples are correct.
bract variant: 'Variable in shape and size' describes variation between bracts, not a quality of one bract. PATO variant means something else (differing from the standard). A
sepal adaxial epidermis hairy: The inner (adaxial) surface of a sepal can be hairy.
spine leaf length: The length of a leaf spine is a valid measurement.
leaf lamina blade-like: 'Ensiform' means sword-shaped. 'Blade-like' is a different PATO meaning, so this is a wrong reading. Use a shape term for ensiform instead.
storage parenchyma color: The colour of flesh (storage tissue) is a valid quality.
petiole semi erect: A petiole can be suberect.
arched: An indusium can be vaulted or arched.
higher order inflorescence axis ciliated: The axis of a higher-order inflorescence, often its apex, can be ciliate.
spikelet female: Grasses and sedges have unisexual (pistillate) spikelets. The examples are correct.
tetrad of microspores present: 'Pollen in tetrads' describes how the pollen is grouped, not whether a tetrad is present. It needs a pollen-unit rule, not 'present'.
branch optical quality: 'Optical quality' is a generic parent term. The examples are really colour and hair cover (lepidote, villous), which have their own terms.
septum complete structure: A septum can be complete or incomplete. The examples are correct.
leaf lamina lobe fringed: Lobes can be fringed with spines or spinules. The examples are correct.
vascular bundle low saturation: Veins can be pale. The examples describe vein colour.
pappus element structure: The PATO term 'structure' is a generic term and does not mean 'connate'. Connate pappus elements are real, but they need a fusion or connation term.
bract fan-shaped: Bracts can be fan-shaped (flabellate).
peduncle pendent: Peduncles can be pendent, for example in fruit. The examples are correct.
seed knobbled: Pebbled or bumpy seed surfaces are common. The examples are correct.
glistening: Spathes can be glossy or shiny.
capitulum inflorescence obconical: Heads (capitula) can be obconic.
leaf lamina condensed: Wrong reading. 'Compressed' means flattened, not 'condensed' (packed denser). A flattened-shape term is needed.
capsule fruit fusiform: Capsules can be fusiform.
flower prolate: Flowers or buds can be ellipsoid (prolate). The examples are correct.
spadix inflorescence constricted: A spadix can be constricted between its sterile and fertile parts.
shoot axis internode slender: Internodes can be slender (grêle).
smooth: Glands and surfaces can be smooth. The examples are correct.
spore capsule operculum hemispheroid: A moss operculum can be hemispherical.
filiform: Lobes and teeth can be filiform.
phyllode leaf present: Phyllodes can be present or absent, so this is a presence statement. 'Phyllodial' on its own is a weaker reading.
mericarp rough: Mericarp surfaces can be rough. The examples are correct.
leaf sheath auricle orbicular: Auricles can be round or orbicular.
recurved: Lobes and apices can be recurved.
spadix inflorescence clavate: A spadix or spadicle can be clavate.
awn non-deciduous (any body part): An awn can be persistent or deciduous.
sepal subcylindrical: Sepals can be subcylindric.
oblong: Pseudobulbs and other organs can be oblong, including compound shapes like ovoid-oblong.
rhomboid: Pinnules and leaflets can be rhombic.
leaf lamina lobe lanceolate-triangular: Lobes can be triangular-lanceolate.
glume deciduous (generic): Glumes can be deciduous or caducous.
2-D shape: '2-D shape' is a generic parent term. The examples have specific shapes (rhombic-hexagonal, polygonal, circular) that should map to specific terms.
anther locule length: Anther locules can be measured for length.
involucral bract deciduous (generic): Involucral bracts can be deciduous.
leaf sheath auricle conspicuous: Auricles can be conspicuous or obvious.
pappus filiform: Pappus bristles can be filiform.
pedicel cuneate: Pedicels can be cuneate (wedge-shaped), as the examples show.
leaf margin fimbriated: Leaf margins can be fimbriate.
pedicel flat: Pedicels can be flattened.
leaf sheath decreased size: Leaf sheaths can be small or reduced. Some examples describe reduction to fibres, which is a different thing.
stalk inconspicuous: A stipe can be indistinct or inconspicuous.
petal base auriculate: A petal base can be auriculate.
perianth spheroid: A perianth can be subglobose.
amount: Bulbil number can be counted, and bulbils can be absent or present.
fertile: Fronds can be fertile or sterile. Some examples add only a length, which is a separate statement.
higher order inflorescence axis diastatic: An inflorescence axis such as a rachilla can disarticulate or not.
higher order inflorescence axis straight: Axes and branches can be straight.
lemma hispid: A lemma can be hispid.
bract adaxial epidermis color: The adaxial surface of a bract or phyllary can have its own colour.
fruit pedicel color: A fruit pedicel can have its own colour.
spheroid: An anther cap can be subglobose.
vascular bundle bristly: Veins can bear bristles, as the examples show.
leaf lamina lobe rectangular: Lobes can be rectangular.
increased thickness: 'Plant organ base' is a generic part with no organ, and the examples are all 'style base'. The bearer should be style, with the base as a position. Same treatme
leaf lamina abaxial epidermis furrowed: Furrowed abaxial surface of the lamina is meaningful and the examples fit.
increased length: Disc length compared with the ovary or flowers is meaningful, and the examples are annotated correctly.
recurved: The orchid epichile is often recurved.
condensed: Wrong reading: 'compressed' here means flattened (dorsiventrally, vertically), not condensed. It needs a flattened or compressed shape term.
keel winged: Winged keels are normal, in the legume keel petal and in keeled structures generally.
fleshy: A fleshy orchid column is a normal character.
megasporophyll tomentose: Cycad megasporophylls are tomentose, and the examples are correct.
costa flat: A moss costa can be flat or broad and flat.
strobilus sessile (sensu botany): A strobilus can be sessile or stalked.
protonema non-deciduous (any body part): 'Persistent' protonema maps to non-deciduous, and the examples fit.
length: Length of a vaginant lamina, including relative length such as 'half the length of the leaf', is meaningful.
petal tessellated: Tessellated (chequered) petals occur, for example in Fritillaria. There is only one flora.
mericarp glandular: A mericarp bearing glandular trichomes is glandular. The examples say so directly.
stamen tapered: Tapering stamens, filament or apex, is meaningful.
truncated: A truncate labellum apex or base is meaningful, and the examples fit.
stipule hispidulous: Hispidulous stipules are normal.
clavate: Clavate vittae are a standard character in Apiaceae fruit descriptions.
legume fruit amount: Wrong bearer: 'seeds per legume' counts the seeds, and 'legume 1 per umbel' is a count of another unit. The count belongs to the counted part (seed) under the c
panicle inflorescence pyramidal: Pyramidal panicles are standard.
acuminate: An acuminate labellum or epichile apex is meaningful.
size: Relative size of labellum lobes (larger, subequal) is meaningful.
seta terminal: Terminal seta (position at the tip) is meaningful.
present: Presence or absence of phyllopodia is the character in the examples.
leaf lamina lobe bifurcated: Bifid or furcate leaf lobes are meaningful.
ligule decurrent: A decurrent ligule base on both sides is meaningful, and the examples fit.
achene fruit spotted: Spotted achenes are normal.
structure: 'Structure' is too generic. The examples say 'proliferous bulbil', which means the bulbil sprouts and is not a structure value. It needs a specific term or the
carpel vestigial: Rudimentary carpels in male flowers are vestigial.
stem keel-shaped: Keeled stems or internodes are meaningful. Some French examples say 'côtelée' (ribbed), a different character.
stem porous: The examples (fibrils and pores, a single pore) look like cell-wall features of hyaline cells, not the stem. Wrong part, and 'a single pore' is a count.
pedicel aggregated: Clustered pedicels are meaningful.
auriculate: An auriculate labellum or lobe is meaningful.
anther low saturation: Pale anthers are a colour intensity. Where a hue is named ('vert pâle'), the hue term should also be taken.
flower irregular spatial pattern: Wrong reading: 'irregular flower' means irregular (zygomorphic) symmetry, not an irregular spatial pattern. It needs the symmetry term.
capsule fruit attenuate: An attenuate capsule base or apex is meaningful.
capitulum inflorescence size: Capitulum size is meaningful.
convex 3-D shape: Disc glands can be turbinate, obovoid or conical.
whole plant tolerant to: Whole-plant tolerance (drought, salt) is meaningful. The stressor must stay in the statement.
stigma fringed: A fringed stigma is meaningful.
receptacle scaphoid: A boat-shaped (naviculaire) receptacle is meaningful, though 'cymbiformes' may refer to scales on it.
cotyledon decreased size: A small cotyledon is meaningful.
capsule fruit ligneous: Woody ('ligneuse') capsules are meaningful.
legume fruit papyraceous: Papery ('papyracée') legume walls are meaningful.
legume fruit glandular: Glandular legumes (glandular hairs on the surface) are meaningful.
drupe fruit tomentose: Tomentose drupes are meaningful.
legume fruit glistening: Glossy or shiny legumes are meaningful.
whole plant depth: Wrong bearer: the depth or thickness belongs to a mat, water or a layer, not the whole plant.
filiform: Rhizophores can be thread-like. 'liliformes' is a typo of 'filiformes'.
shoot system velutinous: Young shoots can be velvety. Some examples say 'velue' (hairy), which is a different term.
caryopsis fruit amount: The examples count caryopses or grains per spikelet or flower. That is a count of another part, not an amount of the caryopsis itself.
shoot axis trichome triangular: The examples are rhizome scales and a leaf shape (deltoid), not trichomes. Triangular trichomes are not a usual character.
shoot axis trichome pilosity: Wrong bearer. The examples describe the hairiness of the shoot axis ('central region glabrous or bearing hairs'), not of a trichome.
shoot axis trichome glabrous: Wrong bearer. 'Central region glabrous' is about the axis or region. A trichome cannot be glabrous.
sorus crowded: Sori can be crowded or closely packed.
leaf lamina tooth prominent: Teeth can be prominent.
lodicule erose: The lodicule (squamella) margin or apex can be erose. The examples are correct.
perigynium truncated: The perigynium base or orifice can be truncate. Some examples describe the beak, which is a sub-part.
thorn blunt: Spines and thorns can be blunt.
megasporangiate strobilus spherical: Seed cones can be globose. One example, 'apex round', is a different shape.
higher order inflorescence axis drooping: Inflorescence branches and rachillae can be pendulous or nodding.
campanulate: A perianth tube can be campanulate.
achene fruit exserted: Achenes can be exserted from the disc or involucre.
achene fruit grooved: Achenes can be grooved or have a dorsal groove.
achene fruit inconspicuous: The examples are about the beak, angles and midnerves, which are other parts. The achene itself is not described as obscure.
achene fruit lanate: Achenes can be woolly.
curved: Corona lobes can be incurved over the style apex.
style low saturation: A style can be pale or pallid. This is a pale colour, which low saturation approximates.
achene fruit cuneate: The achene base can be cuneate.
corolla ascending: Corolla lobes or the limb can be ascending.
seed high brightness: Seeds can be light-coloured or pale.
obtuse: An organ apex can be obtuse or rounded.
bract concealed: Bracts can be hidden by other parts or by perigynia.
bract sharp: The PATO term means an edge that can cut. The examples describe a sharply pointed apex, which is acute or pointed.
involucral bract inconspicuous: The examples describe the midnerves (veins) of the bract, not the bract. The vein is the bearer.
sepal cup-shaped: Sepals can be cup-shaped or cupped.
prominent: The examples are protuberances of a disc, not of the corolla lip. The bearer is wrong.
bark tessellated: Bark can be checkered or tessellated.
sepal cut: Sepals or sepal margins can be incised or cut. The examples are correct.
hydathode superficial: Hydathodes can be superficial or sunken.
hypanthium setose: The hypanthium can be setose.
tubercle diameter: A tubercle has a diameter. The examples are measurements.
attachment quality: The corona can be united to the column or the corolla. The examples are correct.
whole plant dendritic: The examples are about trichomes, not the whole plant. The bearer is wrong.
cincinnus inflorescence circinate: A cincinnus is coiled (circinate).
leaf odorous: Leaves can be fragrant or malodorous.
trichome unicellular: Trichomes can be unicellular.
bract cartilaginous: Bracts or their margins can be cartilaginous.
leaf lamina vein pilosity: Leaf veins can be hairy (strigose, pilose).
seed obconical: The examples are cypselae (fruits), not seeds. The bearer is wrong.
seed dorso-ventrally flattened: Seeds can be flattened dorsiventrally.
erose: A corolla plica margin or summit can be erose.
sepal comparative modifier characteristic: 'Wider' is a comparison between parts (lateral and dorsal sepals), not a quality of one sepal. Pattern 10 or a comparison rule should handle it.
leaf lamina lobe pinnate: Lobes can themselves be pinnately divided.
whole plant sparse: The examples are glands, a cyme and an age effect, not the whole plant. The bearer is wrong.
stem base terete: A stem base can be terete.
leaf lamina tooth antrorse: Teeth can be antrorse.
trichome bulbous: Trichomes can have a bulbous base or tip.
perianth condensed: The PATO term means compact or condensed. The examples mean flattened ('compressed laterally'), which is a different quality.
bracteole dissected: Bracteoles or their margins can be dissected or divided.
scale leaf pilosity: Scale leaves and their margins can be hairy.
scale leaf spotted: Scale leaves can be spotted or dotted, and the examples fit.
leaf transverse orientation: The examples are about veinlets and phyllotaxy, not the leaf. The pair comes from the wrong part.
megasporophyll increased thickness: Megasporophyll parts such as apophyses can be thickened.
elongated: A rostellum can be elongate, and the examples are correct.
broad: Lobes can be broad. The 'broad mouth' example is a different part, but the rest fit.
leaf lamina tooth falciform: Hooked or falcate teeth are a real shape, and the examples fit.
secondary leaf vein hairy: Veins can be hairy, and the examples are correct.
achene fruit low brightness: 'Dark' is a colour description of achenes.
calyx low saturation: 'Pale' is a colour description of the calyx.
glandular: Margins and lobes can be glandular.
tapered: Tapering toward the apex or both ends is a valid shape for this part.
rectangular: Lobes and hypochile can be rectangular.
pedicel inflated: A pedicel can be inflated at the tip. The negated examples are handled by negation.
stigma dissected: A stigma can be divided into parts. A 'lobed' term might fit better, but the reading is correct.
stigma pulvinate: A cushion-shaped stigma is pulvinate.
glandular: Surfaces can be glandular. Negated examples are handled by negation.
leaf margin bristly: A leaf margin can bear bristles.
palea setose: A palea can be setose.
short shoot characteristic: 'Characteristic' is a generic attribute with no information. The examples are 'X or Y' alternatives.
symmetrical: Bases and blades can be symmetrical or equilateral.
bud scale leaf lanceolate: Bud scales can be lanceolate.
tapered: Narrowing toward base and apex is a valid tapered shape.
petiolule velutinous: A petiolule can be velutinous.
plant spore inconspicuous: 'Obscure' describes the surface ornamentation, not the spore. The quality belongs to the sculpture.
linear: Pinnules and blades can be linear.
capitulum inflorescence ovate: The examples say 'ovoid', which is 3-D. Ovate is the 2-D term, so the pair is a wrong reading. Use the ovoid class instead.
leaf sheath auricle elliptic: Auricles can be elliptic.
keel decreased length: A keel can be short.
first order inflorescence axis color: An inflorescence axis can have a colour. The hair-colour examples are weaker, but the pair is valid.
fruit pedicel glabrous: A fruit pedicel can be glabrous.
lateral leaf vein vestigial: Obsolete veins mean the veins are vestigial.
plant ovary rugose: An ovary surface can be rugose.
curvature: A disc or centre can be depressed.
stipule orientation: Stipules can be erect, reflexed or spreading.
banner petal decreased length: The claw of a banner petal can be short.
utricle capsule fruit spotted: Fruits can be spotted or flecked.
utricle capsule fruit smooth: A fruit surface can be smooth.
glume characteristic: 'Characteristic' is generic. The examples are 'X or Y' alternatives that need splitting.
higher order inflorescence axis whorled: Inflorescence branches can be whorled.
strap-shaped: Lobes can be strap-shaped or ligulate.
length: Length is a valid attribute of this part.
secondary xylem high brightness: 'Light' wood means low weight or density, not high brightness. This is a wrong reading of the PATO term.
stipel non-deciduous (any body part): Stipels can be persistent.
microsporophyll width: Microsporophylls have a width. The examples are length × width measurements.
inflorescence axis internode linear: Rachis internodes can be linear.
characteristic: 'Characteristic' is generic. The examples are 'X or Y' alternatives.
peristome tooth transversely striated: Peristome teeth can be cross-striolate.
peristome tooth characteristic: 'Characteristic' is generic. The examples are 'X or Y' alternatives.
strobilus terete: A strobilus or cone can be terete.
leaf base grooved: A canaliculate or channeled leaf base is a groove. The examples fit.
bilobed: A disc can be bilobed, and the examples describe the disc itself.
seed viscid: Sticky or viscid seeds or seed surfaces are real. One example is about sticky hairs on the seed, but the pair is still fine.
bulb drooping: The text 'drop-shaped' was split into 'dro p', and 'drooping' was matched from it. This is a wrong reading, and a drop shape is not drooping.
bracteole subterminal: Subapical or subterminal position of a bracteole is a real position.
corolla plicate: A plicate corolla is real. In some examples only the sinuses are plicate, but the pair is meaningful.
stipule subtriangular: Subtriangular stipules are normal.
tuber increased thickness: Tubers are described as thick. The examples are thickness measurements, so the pair is fine.
bract tricuspidate: Tricuspidate or tridentate bract apices are real.
involucral bract decreased size: Small outer involucral bracts are correct.
plant spore foveate: Foveolate or pitted spore surfaces are standard in pteridophyte descriptions.
amount: 'Styles 2–3 × stylopodium' is a length ratio to another part, not a count. The amount reading is wrong. A ratio rule is needed.
size: Lip size, such as equal or larger than other parts, is a real size statement.
lenticel diameter: Lenticel diameter is correct.
leaf lamina vein pubescent hair: Veins can be pubescent. Some examples describe the leaf surface, but the pair is meaningful.
undulate: An undulate margin is standard.
bud decreased length: Short buds are meaningful. One example is noisy (inflorescence and bud), but the pair is fine.
spore capsule calyptra lobed: A calyptra can be lobed at the base. This is the standard moss description.
lobed: Lobed organs (leaf, corolla, calyx) are common. The depth is a separate matter.
inflorescence axis bent: 'Angled' means with edges (a cross-section shape). It is not bent. The pair comes from a wrong reading.
sporophyll invariant: Uniform sporophylls are meaningful, meaning all of one form.
hypanthium decreased width: A narrow hypanthium or floral tube is correct.
lemma awn amount: A lemma awn count (1-awned, 3-awned) is a real count, and the awn is the bearer.
sharpness: Acute disc lobes or apex are fine.
erect: Erect disc lobes or margins are fine.
spikelet rachilla fragile: A fragile rachilla is a standard grass character.
petiolule decreased size: Small or minute petiolules are correct.
axillary hair length: Hair length is correct.
scale leaf coriaceous: Coriaceous cataphylls or scale leaves are correct.
axillary shoot system elongated: Elongate shoot systems or innovations are fine.
imperforate: Aporose means without pores, which is imperforate, for moss cells and surfaces.
plant embryo vertical: A vertical embryo axis is a real character. The quality is about the embryo's orientation.
unilateral: A unilateral disc is a real character, with the disc on one side.
hilum centered: A central hilum is correct.
seed pyramidal: Pyramidal or tetrahedral seeds are real.
receptacle velutinous: French 'velu' means hairy or villous. It is not velvety (velutinous), so the reading is wrong. Map it to the villous or hairy term.
flower pedicel pubescent hair: Pubescent or pubérulent pedicels are correct.
secondary leaf vein spatial pattern: Reticulate venation pattern of secondary veins is meaningful.
first order inflorescence axis diameter: Axis diameter is correct.
flower nectary length: Nectary length is correct.
pappus element straight: Straight pappus bristles are correct.
pollen sac spatial pattern: Pollen sacs in one row or in pairs are an arrangement pattern. Some examples show a different part (crown), but the pair is fine.
plant gall present: The text 'fruits à galles' says the host organ has galls. The gall itself is not 'present'. Presence belongs on the host organ.
shoot axis trichome filiform: A filiform apex of a trichome or scale is correct.
paraphysis width: Paraphysis width is correct.
shoot axis trichome deciduous (generic): Deciduous or caducous scales and trichomes are real.
circular: A circular staminal disc is correct.
broad: '2.5–4.5 cm broad' is a measured width. It belongs to a width quality, not to the 'broad' shape term.
perigynium striated: A striate perigynium (many-nerved) is a standard sedge character.
lodicule attenuate: Attenuate lodicules are meaningful.
fertile lemma obtuse: An obtuse fertile lemma is correct.
bract rose colour: Rose-coloured bracts or bract tips are correct.
amount: Stomatal rows or lines are counted (4-7 rows, 2 or 3 lines), so a count quality fits.
peduncle deciduous (generic): A scape or peduncle can be deciduous or fall off with the leaves. The examples fit.
filament smooth: Filaments can have a smooth surface, as opposed to hairy or papillose.
mericarp rugose: A mericarp surface can be rugose. 'Corrugated' is close enough.
mericarp striated: A mericarp can be striate or ridged. The French 'striés' fits.
palea spiny: A palea can have spinulose keels or tips. 'Not spinose' is a negation that the rules for negation handle.
inflorescence axis glandular: An inflorescence axis can be glandular or stipitate-glandular.
sharpness: An apex can be sharp (acute, acuminate). The sharpness attribute is a reasonable parent for these values.
sessile (sensu botany): A gynostegium can be sessile or subsessile, which is the botanical sense of 'sessile'.
condensed: Wrong reading. The PATO term 'condensed' means compact, but the examples mean flattened ('compressed'). Use the flattened or compressed term.
bracteole condensed: Wrong reading. 'Condensed' means compact, but 'compressed' here means flattened. Map to the flattened or compressed term.
length: Ray laminae have a length, and the examples are measurements.
bracteole hispidulous: A bracteole can be hispidulous (finely bristly).
pedicel horizontal: A pedicel can be horizontal. The examples fit.
perianth bristly: Wrong reading. 'Perianth bristles' are bristles as parts (the perianth reduced to bristles), not a bristly surface. 'Bristlelike' is a shape. Annotate them as a
trichome optical quality: Trichomes can be translucent, transparent or coloured. The generic optical quality is acceptable here, though a colour or transparency term would be finer.
spore capsule calyptra ciliated: A calyptra can be ciliate at the base.
perigynium spotted: A perigynium can be dotted or spotted with colour.
spike inflorescence overlapping: Spikes can overlap each other.
achene fruit optical quality: The examples are achene colours (pale to dark brown). A colour term would be finer, but the pair is meaningful.
inflorescence radiating: A head or inflorescence can be radiant (radiate, with rays).
bracteole erose: Bracteole margins can be erose.
leaf pentagonal: A leaf blade can be pentagonal.
concave 3-D shape: Hooded or cucullate lobes are a concave three-dimensional shape.
tepal erose: Tepal margins can be erose.
involucre spreading: Involucre teeth or apices can spread.
seed mealy: A seed can be mealy (farinose), and the endosperm texture is described the same way.
short shoot blunt: Wrong part. 'Spur blunt' describes a spur, not the short shoot. The bearer should be the spur.
spine leaf orientation: Spines can be porrect or descending, which is an orientation.
thorn size: Thorns, spines or prickles can be unequal in size.
seed subterminal: Wrong part. 'Hilum subterminal' describes the position of the hilum, not of the seed. The bearer should be the hilum.
obtuse: Wrong reading. 'Rounded' is a different shape from obtuse, and the PATO term means an obtuse angle.
keel-shaped: Carinate or keeled lobes or midveins are keel-shaped.
length: The examples are length measurements of the part.
lobed: Parts with a margin can be lobed. 'Unlobed' is a negation handled by the rules.
ray flower position: Ray flowers can be ascending, spreading or appressed, which are positions.
leaf sheath translucent: A leaf sheath can be translucent.
constricted: Parts can be constricted at the middle or distally.
nectary increased thickness: A nectary can be thick or thickened.
portion of secretory tissue characteristic: 'Characteristic' is too generic. The examples mix margins, glands and lobes, so the pair says nothing.
perianth characteristic: 'Characteristic' is too generic. The examples are wings, bristles and lobes, which are other parts and qualities.
entire: A margin can be entire.
glabrous: Spathes and similar parts can be glabrous.
broad: Lobes and margins can be broad.
seed D-shaped: A seed can be D-shaped.
seed coat increased thickness: A seed coat can be thick, and the French 'épais' matches.
shoot system spiny: A shoot system can be spiny or thorny.
calyx plicate: A calyx or its limb can be plicate.
mericarp flattened: A mericarp can be flattened.
linear: Lobes, scales and apices can be linear.
sporangium attachment quality: A sporangium can be sessile or stalked.
pedicel pendent: A pedicel can be pendent.
seed centered: Wrong part. 'Hile central' and 'umbo subcentral' describe the hilum or umbo, not the seed as a whole. The bearer should be the hilum.
branch irregular spatial pattern: Branching can be irregular. One example (irregular stripes) is a different thing, but the others fit.
short shoot reflexed: Wrong part. 'spur' here is the spur of a flower or petal (as in Aquilegia, orchids), not a short shoot. The bearer should be a spur class.
straight: A pollinium (pollinarium) can be straight or bent.
spreading: Rostellum lobes can spread or diverge. The bare 'slightly spreading' example has no clear bearer.
caudate: A corolla lip can end in a tail-like (caudate) apex. Some examples may really be about the apex, not the lip.
petiole adaxial epidermis pubescent hair: The adaxial surface of a petiole can be pubescent. The examples are correct.
whole plant elongated: The examples (soboles, tubercles, creeping parts) describe organs of the plant, not the whole plant. Whole-plant shape is not elongated in the intended sense; t
width: A cupule has a width.
bark high brightness: Bark colour can be light or pale ('light coloured', 'claire').
leaf lamina tip blunt: A leaf lamina tip can be blunt.
prickle retrorse: Prickles are described as retrorse (pointing backwards).
higher order inflorescence axis branched: Higher-order inflorescence axes can be branched or forked.
flower nectary quadrangular: Nectar scales and nectaries can be quadrangular or subquadrangular.
peristome inserted into: The examples give the insertion position of the peristome relative to the mouth. They do not say it is inserted into something. The PATO term is the wrong readi
concave 3-D shape: A spathe can be hooded, saccate or urceolate (concave).
leaf lamina lobe erose: The margin of a leaf lamina lobe can be erose. The quality is taken from the margin onto the lobe.
oblong: A tree crown can be oblong.
sepal cream: Sepals can be cream coloured.
petal circinate: The examples describe the spur of the petal ('petaline spur circinate'). The spur is its own part, so petal is the wrong bearer.
lamina decreased width: A lamina can be narrow. One example is about wings of the lamina, which is a different part.
lemma lanate: A lemma can be lanate or woolly.
lemma bristly: A lemma can be bristly.
discontinuous: An indusium can be interrupted or discontinuous.
tepal characteristic: PATO_0000001 is the generic root 'quality'. The examples are about margins (entire, erose, incised), which have their own terms.
falciform: Labellum lobes can be falcate (sickle-shaped).
ray flower hispid: Ray flowers (ray florets) can be hispid.
inflorescence aromatic: An inflorescence can be aromatic or scented. A statement naming a specific scent (carrots, prunes) is a different quality.
mesocarp succulent: A mesocarp can be succulent.
petal base truncated: A petal base can be truncate.
inflorescence bract linear: Inflorescence bracts (spathelles) can be linear.
plant spore subspherical: Spores can be subspherical.
leaflet lanceolate-triangular: Deltoid-lanceolate is a triangular-lanceolate shape, and a leaflet can have it.
leaflet regular spatial pattern: Leaflets can be regularly arranged. The pattern describes the arrangement of leaflets.
auriculate: A spathe can be auriculate. One example mentions a throat margin, which may be another organ.
anther theca sessile (sensu botany): Anther thecae can be sessile.
tubular: A spathe can be tubular.
inflorescence axis internode pilosity: Inflorescence axis internodes can be glabrous or hairy.
pilosity: A perianth tube can be hairy or glabrous, inside or outside.
plant ovary spotted: An ovary can be spotted or dotted. One example ('and spots') has no clear bearer.
guard cell length: A guard cell has a length.
pappus element has fewer parts of type: 'Few' counts how many elements the pappus has. It is not a quality of one element. The count belongs to the pappus or the counted-parts rule.
areole bud size: The examples are about areoles (cactus), not areole buds. The part is wrong. Equal or unequal size also describes a group.
involucral bract has fewer parts of type: 'Phyllaries few' counts the bracts of the involucre. It is not a quality of a single bract. The counted-parts rule should take it.
leaf sheath auricle undulate: A leaf sheath auricle can be undulate.
leaf sheath auricle diameter: A leaf sheath auricle has a diameter.
gemma clavate: Gemmae can be clavate.
fruit plicate: A fruit (such as a loment) can be plicate.
pedicel decreased strength: A pedicel can be weak. There are only two statements.
leaf apex retuse: A leaf apex can be retuse.
bracteole sepal-like: A bracteole can be sepal-like (sepaloid).
sporangium sessile (sensu botany): Sporangia can be sessile.
cuspidate: A corolla lip can have a cuspidate apex. Some examples may be about the apex.
spheroid: Pseudobulbs can be subglobose or spheroid.
ray flower filiform: Ray flowers can be filiform.
pappus increased amount: Pappus can be copious or scanty. The examples are annotated correctly.
triangular: The viscidium can be triangular, and the examples agree.
costa characteristic: PATO_0000001 'quality' is the generic root. The examples (smooth, toothed, papillose) are surface or margin states and need their own specific terms.
cauline leaf length: Length of a cauline leaf is meaningful. Some examples include the petiole, which is a minor issue.
glume tapered: A glume can be tapered or narrowed to the apex.
leaf lamina tooth inconspicuous: Teeth can be inconspicuous or indistinct.
elliptic: The epichile can be elliptic, and the examples agree.
leaf lamina tooth conical: A tooth can be conical. 'conic lumens' is a wrong example (it refers to cells), but the pair is valid.
linear: Corona lobes and scales can be linear.
sepal apex cuspidate: A sepal apex can be cuspidate.
lateral leaf vein length: Vein length is meaningful. Some examples describe where the vein arises rather than its length.
characteristic: PATO_0000001 is the generic quality root. 'entire' and 'serrate' are margin shapes that should use specific terms.
sepal margin velutinous: A margin can be velutinous (velvety hairy).
branch banded: A branch or its bark can be striped or banded.
leaf lamina drooping: A leaf lamina can droop or be pendulous.
flattened: Flattened applies to many organs, such as stems and fruits, including dorsiventrally flattened ones.
leaf apex sharp: A leaf apex can be sharp or sharply pointed.
gemma amount: Gemmae are counted per cluster or per axil.
spore capsule operculum straight: An operculum or its beak can be straight.
plant cell rhomboid: Cell shape can be rhomboid, as in moss laminal cells.
raceme inflorescence inflexible: A raceme can be stiff or inflexible.
sorus increased thickness: Sori can be thick.
pilosity: Hairiness types (puberulent, villous, hirsute) apply to this anatomy class.
height: The height of a basal membrane is a valid measurement.
leaf midvein protruding: A midvein can protrude. The negated examples ('not projecting') need negation handling, but the pair is valid.
amount: Glochids are counted per side or per area.
short shoot tubular: The examples describe a 'spur' (a floral part), not a short shoot. The pair comes from a wrong part reading.
root nodule transparent: 'axillary hyaline nodules' are moss structures, not root nodules, and 'hyaline' is not a quality of a root nodule. The pair rests on a wrong reading.
dentated: A margin can be dentate or denticulate.
flower rose colour: A flower can be rose coloured.
concave: Lobes and lips can be concave.
increased length: Caudicles can be long.
decreased length: Caudicles can be short.
stem base furrowed: 'Fluted' at the base of a trunk is a furrowed surface. This is acceptable as a stem base shape.
torsioned: An orchid column can be twisted.
tuber increased size: A tuber can be enlarged or large.
nectary elongated: A nectary can be elongated.
spore capsule operculum increased length: Operculum length is meaningful. Several examples describe the beak length, which is a minor imprecision.
plant ovary pulvinate: An ovary can be pulvinate (cushion-like).
plant ovary flat: An ovary or its apex can be flat.
plant ovary subovoid: An ovary can be subovoid.
plant ovary concealed: An ovary can be concealed in the disk.
plant ovary furrowed: An ovary can be furrowed (sillonné).
circular: A disk can be circular.
inconspicuous: Calyx lobes can be inconspicuous.
undulate: Calyx lobes can be undulate.
raceme inflorescence pedunculate: A raceme can be pedunculate, meaning it has a stalk.
anther oblique orientation: Anther orientation can be oblique or inclined.
stalk increased size: A stalk (stipe) can be large or enlarged.
filament setose: A filament can be setose or setulose. The French 'sétuleux' is slightly finer than setose, a minor imprecision.
height: An androgynophore has a height.
leaf lamina base length: The length of a pseudopetiole (a leaf base part) is meaningful.
leaf collar smooth: A leaf collar can be smooth.
leaf adaxial epidermis sericeous: A leaf epidermis surface can be sericeous (silky).
style fibrillary: 'capillary' means thin and hair-like, which is a shape. PATO fibrillary means something else, so the pair rests on a wrong reading of the term.
connective decreased length: A connective or its appendage can be short.
short shoot entire: 'Spur' here is a floral or petal spur or a leaf-like margin, not a short shoot. The pair exists only through a wrong reading of the part.
bracteole ascending: Bracteoles can be ascending.
fruit ring shaped: The examples describe an annular scar or node on the fruit. The scar is ring-shaped, not the fruit.
achene fruit clavate: Achenes can be clavate, and the examples are correct.
flower pedicel amount: Pedicel counts per umbellet are a normal counted-part case.
banner petal sericeous: A standard petal can be sericeous.
samara fruit pubescent hair: Samaras can be pubescent. One example is about the stigmatic surface, but the pair is fine.
spherical: Globose traps are spherical, so the pair is meaningful.
strap-shaped: Ligulate or strap-shaped lobes are normal.
decreased size: Small glands are a normal size statement.
amount: Counts of cyathia per cyme are a counted-part case.
spore capsule operculum differentiated: In mosses an operculum is either differentiated or not from the capsule. This is a correct use.
present: Pseudoparaphyllia can be present or absent.
leaf apex rough: A leaf apex can be rough or roughened.
leaf apex broad: A leaf apex or acumen can be broad.
spore capsule calyptra entire: A calyptra base can be entire, since the margin is entire.
axillary shoot system structure: 'Evenly foliate' is about how leaves are arranged, not about a structure quality of the shoot system. The generic PATO structure term is the wrong reading.
leaf lamina intramarginal vein sunken: Veins are sunken on the upper side of a leaf, and the examples are correct.
height: A height measurement of a part, such as a leaf scar, is meaningful.
lamina scalloped: A lamina margin can be crenate or crenulate (scalloped). The margin would be the better bearer, but the pair is meaningful.
leaf colored: Leaves can be coloured, for example by anthocyanin.
seedling pilosity: Seedlings can be hairy, puberulent or glabrescent.
stipule duration: Stipules are caducous, fugacious or persistent, which is a duration.
pappus element ciliated: Pappus elements (bristles) can be ciliate.
secondary leaf vein structure: The examples say the veins are joined or confluent, a connection between veins. The generic structure term is the wrong reading.
cyme inflorescence dense: A cyme can be dense.
keel petal length: A keel petal has a length.
slender: Slender lobes and teeth are meaningful.
branched: Chains and hairs can be branched or forked.
broad: Parts can be broad, and a width in mm is also fine.
obovate: Lobes and similar parts can be obovate.
quadrangular: Pseudobulbs and stems can be four-angled.
pistillate flower width: A flower has a width.
increased size: Drupelets can be large.
decreased width: An androphore can be narrow.
position: Domatia are described by position, such as axillary.
hypanthium tapered: A hypanthium narrows into a neck, so it can be tapered.
petiolule terete: Petiolules can be terete.

plant sap present: Sap can be present or absent.
flat: A staminal disc can be flat.
shoot axis trichome unstructured: 'Subentire' is a margin shape. It is read as 'unstructured', and the part is wrong.
color: Colour is meaningful for the part.
sepal trumpet-shaped: A sepal can be trumpet-shaped. 'Bucciniform' is a close match.
branch dendritic: The dendritic or stellate hairs belong to the trichomes, not the branch. 'Dendroid' for a branch means tree-like, which is a different meaning.
keel petal curved: A keel petal can be arcuate or curved.
trichome retrorse: Trichomes can be retrorse.
plant ovary entire: The examples describe the margins of stigma or style lobes or the crown, not the ovary. The ovary wall is not described as entire.
plant ovary dentated: The examples describe a toothed apex or crown margin, which belongs to another part. An ovary is not dentate.
pappus height: The height of a pappus crown is meaningful.
leaf base increased width: A leaf base can be broadened.
leaf semi-deciduous(plant): Leaves are semi-evergreen or semi-deciduous.
2-D shape: Appendages and lobes can be ovate.
increased length: Corona lobes and filaments can be long.
cladode linear: Linear cladodes are a normal shape description, as in Asparagus and Ruscus. The examples are correct.
leaf lamina tooth irregular spatial pattern: Irregular spacing or irregular size of teeth is meaningful, and the examples fit it.
quadrangular: Lobes and lips can be subquadrangular, and the examples are correct. The part in the FLOPO class was not looked up. Check that it is a lobe or lip class.

perigynium ciliated: Perigynium margins are often ciliate (Carex), and the examples are correct.

spike inflorescence tapered: A spike can taper at its base, and the examples are correct.
bud scale leaf hairy: Bud scales can be hairy. In some examples the hairs are on midribs, which is a small loss of detail, but the pair is fine.
coma deciduous (generic): A coma (tuft of hairs on a seed) can fall off easily or not. The examples are correct.
increased size: Enlarged pinnules are meaningful (for example enlarged basiscopic pinnules in ferns), and the examples are correct.
leaf lamina tooth linear: Linear teeth are meaningful, and the examples are correct.

petal ratio: Petal length-to-width ratio is meaningful, and the examples are correct.
inflorescence bract present: Presence or absence of inflorescence bracts is meaningful. A few examples, such as '3d scale absent', are about other parts, but the pair is fine.
leaf lamina semicircular: Semicircular or semiorbicular leaf blades are normal, and the examples are correct. One example, 'sinus semicircular', belongs to the sinus.
stigma ratio: The width-to-length ratio of a stigma is meaningful, and the examples are correct.
