bulb subcylindrical: A bulb can be subcylindrical.
tepal retuse: Tepal apices can be retuse.
diameter: A synandrium (fused androecium) is a round or discoid structure, and its diameter is given in mm.
fruit pedicel dilated: A fruit pedicel can be dilated, usually at the apex.
oblong: A pseudostaminode can be oblong.
clavate: Pseudobulbs are often clavate. The examples are correct.
leaf lamina lobe notched: A leaf lamina lobe can be notched at the apex or margin.
cuneate: An orchid labellum can be cuneate.
concave: A spathe can be concave.
scale leaf low saturation: 'Pale' is low colour saturation, and a scale leaf (cataphyll) can be pale. Some examples carry a hue as well, which a colour rule should split off.
ligule inflexible: A ligule can be rigid or stiff. A few examples are about hairs on the ligule, not the ligule itself.
leaf sheath auricle clasping: Leaf sheath auricles can be clasping (amplexicaul).
shape: Floral disc lobes have shapes such as semiorbicular, ovoid and conic. The apex fragments (retuse, mucronate) belong to apex shape, not this pair.
ridged: A perispore can have ridges (lophate). The 'without ridges' example needs a negation check.
orientation: Pinnules can be ascending, spreading or descending.
obconical: A floral disc, or its lobes, can be obconical. The lobes also have their own class.
dissected: A floral disc can be divided or dissected into lobes. The example 'each divided by a septum' is about the ovary and should not be counted.
leaf nodular: A leaf can bear nodules or be nodular on its surface.
petal apex dentated: A petal apex can be toothed or dentate.
width: A spadix appendix has a width, given as 'length × width' or 'larges de ...'.
tuber decreased size: A tuber or tuberoid can be small.
cylindrical: A spathe tube can be cylindrical.
utricle capsule fruit sessile (sensu botany): A fruit can be sessile or subsessile. The PO class is a utricle, a one-seeded fruit that is not a capsule, but the pair is fine.
width: A calyx tube has a width. 'Long et de large' gives length and width together, which a dimension rule should split.
leaf subtriangular: A leaf can be subtriangular. 'Furrow subtriangular' is a different part.
connective strap-shaped: An anther connective can be strap- or tongue-shaped.
cladode flat: A cladode (phylloclade) is flat.
keel fimbriated: A keel can be fimbriate, and so can its appendages.
symmetry: A pinna or its base can be symmetrical or asymmetrical.
plant embryo spatial pattern: Wrong reading. 'Solitary' for an embryo means one embryo (a count, as in polyembryony), not a spatial pattern. It belongs to the count pattern.
phyllome lamina lobe 2-D shape: A lamina lobe can be ovate, oblong or deltoid.
truncated: The base of a plant organ can be truncate.
shoot axis internode curved: Internodes can be curved or arcuate.
prophyll keel-shaped: A prophyll can be keeled. The keel count ('2-keeled') should go to the count pattern.
lodicule elliptic: A lodicule can be elliptic.
lodicule increased thickness: A lodicule can be thickened or thick, often at the base.
caryopsis fruit convex 3-D shape: A caryopsis can be obovoid.
fruit subtriangular: A fruit can be subtriangular or subtrigonous. The 'abaxial wing' example is another part.
capsule fruit clavate: A capsule can be clavate.
size: A floral corona can be reduced in size. The value is 'reduced', so the pair should map to the small or reduced size value.
plant ovary subulate: An ovary can be subulate.
anther bent: An anther can be bent or geniculate.
plant ovule convex 3-D shape: An ovule can be obovoid, ovoid or ellipsoid.
lanceolate: A frond can be lanceolate.
glume fringed: A glume can be fringed, usually along the margin with hairs.
scalloped: A corolla lobe can be crenulate or scalloped at the margin.
higher order inflorescence axis conspicuous: An inflorescence axis such as a rachilla can be conspicuous or visible.
subcylindrical: A gynostemium (orchid column) can be subcylindrical.
discoid: A stylopodium can be disc-shaped.
spotted: A floral disc can be spotted with dots.
glabrous: A gynostemium can be glabrous.
fimbriated: A labellum lobe margin can be fimbriate.
legume fruit convex 3-D shape: A legume can be ovoid or obovoid.
lanceolate: Lobes and labella are lanceolate; the examples fit.
utricle capsule fruit hairy: Fruits and their parts (keels, distal part) can be hairy.
nut fruit attenuate: Nut base or apex can be attenuate.
nut fruit surrounded by: Nutlets are enveloped by the utricle. This is a real relation between the two parts, though the target part is not recorded.
leaf lamina base plicate: A leaf base can be plicate (pleated).
nut fruit curved: Nuts can be curved.
glume hard: Glume hardness is a standard grass character.
oblong: Disk lobes can be oblong.
2-D shape: This is the generic shape attribute, used where the text gives a range such as 'oblong to elliptic'. Disk lobes have a shape.
ciliated: Perianth lobes can be ciliate.
leaf lamina vein sparse: Veinlet density is described as sparse or dense.
color: The hypochile has a colour.
receptacle bent: Receptacles can be bent. 'angled' is a slightly different reading but acceptable.
sepal decreased depth: 'Shallow' describes the depth of teeth, lobes or incisions, not the sepal. The reading is wrong. A rule for lobe or sinus depth is needed instead.
pilosity: Pilosity is the hairiness attribute, with values such as pilose, villous and glabrous.
caryopsis fruit width: Caryopsis width, as a measurement.
lemma sericeous: A lemma can be sericeous.
leaf fringed: Leaves and leaf sheaths can have a fringed margin.
elongated: The disk can be elongated.
stalk decreased size: A stalk can be small. The size is vague but meaningful.
short shoot truncated: The examples are about a spur ('spur broad and truncate'). The part is probably a wrong mapping of 'spur' to short shoot.
truncated: Anther caps, margins and apices can be truncate.
root inflated: Roots and root tubers can be inflated.
lateral leaf vein pilosity: Leaf veins can be hairy (pilose or hirsute).
bifurcated: Fronds and pinnae can be forked.
involucre decreased length: The involucre can be short. Some examples describe the peduncle, but the first one is correct.
short shoot decreased thickness: The examples are about a spur ('éperon mince'). The part is probably a wrong mapping of 'spur' to short shoot.
microsporophyll cuneate: Microsporophylls are leaf-like and can be cuneate.
scale leaf tomentose: Scale leaves can be tomentose.
plant ovule color: Ovules have a colour.
perforate: A condyle can be perforate.
discoid: A cupule can be discoid.
vascular bundle ciliated: The examples are margins and veins of leaves or lobes. 'Vascular bundle' is a wrong mapping of 'vein', and a bundle is internal and cannot be ciliate.
pedicel fused with: Pedicels can be fused to the internode or to each other.
pubescent hair: The corona can be pubescent.
higher order inflorescence axis quadrangular: Rachillae and inflorescence axes can be quadrangular.
height: Height is a normal measurement.
bowl shaped: Cups, calyces and similar parts can be bowl-shaped.
scale leaf tubular: Cataphylls (scale leaves) can be tubular.
sparse: Frond spacing can be sparse.
receptacle filiform: Receptacle bristles are filiform. The quality belongs to the bristles, but the receptacle reading is acceptable.
stem node hispid: Stem nodes can be hispid.
fruit valve width: Fruit valve width is a measurement. Some examples are notch widths, which is a minor mix.
heart shaped: Leaf or frond bases can be cordate.
leaf lamina vein color: Veinlets have a colour.
plant spore oblong: Spores can be oblong in outline.
leaf wilty: Leaves can be wilted at anthesis.
nut fruit structure: 'Structure' is too generic. The examples are about a margin or wing on the nut, which needs a specific margin or wing term.
spike inflorescence curved: Spikes can be curved.

stomatal complex has fewer parts of type: 'Stomata few' is the number of stomata on a surface, not the number of parts of a stomatal complex. The reading is wrong. A rule for stomatal density would be n
gynoecium terete: A gynoecium or pistil can be terete.
lemma deciduous (generic): A lemma can be deciduous.
leaf base entire: A leaf base margin can be entire.
dilated: A base can be dilated.
style strap-shaped: Styles and style branches can be strap-shaped (ligulate).
petal plicate: Petals and corolla parts can be plicate (pleated).
seed velutinous: Seed surfaces can be velvety.
linear: Caudicles (orchid pollinium stalks) can be linear.
leaf lamina lobe parallelodromous: Parallelodromous is a venation pattern. The examples say the lobes lie parallel to each other, which is orientation, so this is a wrong reading.
paraphysis obconical: A paraphysis can have an obconical head. The examples name the head, so the quality is really on a sub-part, but it is acceptable.
costa keel-shaped: A costa (moss midrib) can be keeled in cross-section.
arillode present: Presence of an arillode is a normal character. The examples are correct.
tomentose: An androgynophore can be tomentose.
star shaped: A floral corona, or its lobes, can be stellate. 'Spreading' in the examples is a separate orientation term.
glabrous: Style branches can be glabrous.
decreased length: Corona lobes can be short. Comparisons such as 'shorter than anthers' are acceptable.
leaflet trapezoid: Leaflets can be trapezoid.
subcircular: Leaf scars can be subcircular.
fruit pedicel decreased length: A fruit pedicel can be short.
2-D shape: The generic shape attribute fits compound shapes such as deltoid-elliptic on leaf scars.
triangular: Leaf scars can be triangular or deltoid.
leaf tricuspidate: A leaf (apex or margin) can be tri-toothed or tricuspidate. The examples are acceptable.
cyme inflorescence pilosity: Cymes can be hairy. The examples are indumentum types, so the attribute is acceptable.
stem node distance: 'Nodes 2-7 cm apart' gives the internode length, not a property of the node. Use internode length instead.
stipule cup-shaped: Stipules can be cup-shaped.
epicalyx entire: An epicalyx can have an entire margin or entire lobes. The examples are mostly about the margin.
inflorescence brush-like shape: Inflorescences can be brush-like.
lamina dissected: A lamina can be dissected.
valve torsioned: Valves can be twisted.
triangular: Fronds can be triangular or deltoid in outline.
locule width: A locule has a width. Some examples are dimension pairs, but they are acceptable.
androecium prolate: The examples say 'ellipsoid', which is a different shape from prolate. This is a wrong reading. Use the ellipsoid term.
shoot system ridged: Shoot systems can be ridged.
lanceolate-triangular: Corolla lobes can be lanceolate-triangular. This is a compound shape that exists in PATO.
decreased length: A spathe can be short. Some examples refer to the neck, which is a sub-part.
cauline leaf lanceolate: Cauline leaves can be lanceolate.
spikelet floret amount: The counts are of stamens, stigmas and lodicules inside the floret, not of florets. This is the wrong part.
follicle fruit tomentose: Follicles can be tomentose.
staminode terete: Staminodes can be terete.
capsule fruit decreased width: A capsule can be narrow. Some examples refer to the neck, urn or teeth, which are sub-parts.
flower bract decreased length: A flower bract can be short or shorter than the sepals.
2-D shape: Disc glands can have a 2-D shape such as rotund or ovate.
pubescent hair: A spathe can be pubescent.
increased length: A spadix appendix can be long.
leaf collar texture: A grass leaf collar can be scabrid or smooth. The texture attribute fits.
palea knobbled: A palea can be minutely bumpy. Knobbled is a loose match.
trichome papyraceous: Trichomes are not papery. The example probably describes a bract or scale, so this is the wrong part.
spatulate: An orchid labellum can be spatulate.
leaflet variant: Leaflets can vary. The variant term is generic but acceptable.
flower nectary amount: Nectaries, such as nectar scales, can be counted.
peristome tooth bifurcated: Peristome teeth can be bifid.
stem node bent: Stem nodes can be geniculate (bent).
leaf apex decreased length: A leaf apex, including its acumen or apiculus, can be short.
ligule non-deciduous (any body part): Ligules can be persistent or not.
spikelet pedunculate: Spikelets can be pedunculate.
shoot axis internode spiny: Internodes can be spiny or prickly.
hypanthium spiny: A hypanthium can be prickly.
calyx translucent: A calyx can be translucent.
flower ring shaped: The annular part is the floral disk, not the whole flower. This is the wrong part. The pair belongs on the disk.
leaf lamina base spur shaped: 'Base spurred' says the base bears a spur. It does not say the base is spur-shaped, so this is a wrong reading.
seed fringed: Seeds can have a fringe of hairs or scales. Some examples describe the margin, not the seed, so they should be checked.
root blunt: A root apex can be blunt.
first order inflorescence axis glabrous: A rachis or inflorescence axis can be glabrous.
petal subtriangular: Petals and petal lobes can be subtriangular.
shoot axis internode present: The examples are lengths, 'solid' or 'almost absent'. None of them state that internodes are present. The pair comes from a wrong reading.
involucral bract glaucous: Involucral bracts can be glaucous or pruinose. The 'not glaucous' example is a negation, which is fine.
secondary xylem aromatic: Wood can be aromatic. Some examples say 'offensive smell', which is a different quality, so check those.
rhizoid simple: Rhizoids can be simple (unbranched).
capitulum inflorescence tomentose: Capitula and involucres can be tomentose.
sepal wrinkled: Sepals can be wrinkled.
coma increased length: A coma (hair tuft on a seed) has a length, and 'long' is correct.
anther porous: Anthers that open by pores (poricidal) are porous.
diameter: Diameter is a normal attribute for round parts such as bulbils. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
texture: A scarious (dry, membranous) margin is a texture. Check that the bearer is the margin.
spike inflorescence fusiform: Spikes can be fusiform.
shoot axis internode filiform: Internodes can be filiform. Some examples also describe pedicels, so check those.
raceme inflorescence structure: The examples say sessile or pedunculate, or elongating in fruit. They describe the stalk and growth, not 'structure'. The pair comes from a wrong reading.
stipule open: Stipules can be open or closed (sheathing) at the base.
alar cell size: Alar cells can be small or large.
plant cell decreased length: Cells can be short.
central strand decreased size: A central strand can be small. Some examples describe its cells, not the strand.
position: Perichaetia can be terminal, lateral or axillary, which is position.
peristome striated: A peristome surface can be striolate (finely striate).
gemma fusiform: Gemmae can be fusiform.
alar cell obtuse: The examples say 'rounded', not obtuse. Obtuse is an angle or apex term and does not fit a cell group.
plant epidermal cell amount: Epidermal cells can be counted in rows. This fits the counted-parts rule.
length: Length is a normal attribute for a basal membrane or tooth. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
peristome tooth truncated: Peristome teeth can be truncate.
whole plant color brightness: A whole plant can be light or dark green. Brightness is a reasonable attribute for this.
meristematic apical cell smooth: The examples are about apical leaf cells being smooth, not the meristematic apical cell. The part is the wrong one.
peristome transversely striated: A peristome can be cross-striolate.
keel-shaped: Keeled parts are common, such as bracts and glumes. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
peristome tooth increased thickness: Peristome teeth can be thick or thickened. Some examples ('stout', 'spirally thickened') are a different meaning.
porous: Porose parts, such as hyaline cells with pores, are valid. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
sporangium base width: The sporangium base can have a width.
scale leaf shedability: Scale leaves (cataphylls) can be deciduous or persistent.
shriveled: Shrivelling is a valid quality for parts such as petals and fruits. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
endosperm increased thickness: Endosperm can be thick.
legume fruit size: Legumes can be large or small.
bracteole unilateral: Bracteoles can be unilateral (one-sided).
drupe fruit asymmetrical: Drupes can be asymmetrical.
capsule fruit fleshy: Capsule walls can be fleshy.
winged: Winged parts, such as lobes, stems and fruits, are valid. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
inflorescence bipartite: 'Cyme bipare' is a branching type (two branches). The PATO term means divided into two parts, so it is a wrong reading. This belongs in a branching rule.
pistillode cup-shaped: A pistillode can be cup-shaped.
anther sinuous: Anther thecae can be sinuous. The bearer may be the theca (loge), not the whole anther.
flower pedicel pilosity: A pedicel can be hairy or glabrous, so pilosity applies.
spike inflorescence conical: Spikes can be conical.
oblique orientation: Oblique orientation is valid for lobes and similar parts. The part label is empty, so the part should be confirmed.
petiolule rugose: A petiolule can be rough or rugose.
primary leaf vein position: Position of the primary vein, such as median or lateral, is valid.
legume fruit depth: The examples are 'd'épaisseur' (thickness) and 'de côté' (side). Depth is the wrong PATO term. Use thickness or width.
inflorescence dissected: Inflorescences are divided or dissected; 'divisée dès la base' fits.
first order inflorescence axis angular: Inflorescence axes and rachis can be angular; the examples fit.
panicle inflorescence decreased length: A short panicle is meaningful. One example ('rameaux très courts') is about branches, not the panicle.
banner petal inconspicuous: The examples describe appendices, not the banner petal. This is a wrong part reading.
banner petal decreased size: The examples describe small appendices, not the banner petal itself. This is a wrong part reading.
banner petal velutinous: A banner petal can be densely silky-hairy ('étendard velu-soyeux'). The velutinous term is a slightly loose match for silky.
increased thickness: Measured thicknesses ('8 cm thick') belong to thickness with a value, not to 'increased thickness', which is a comparison.
dense: Dense foliage or canopy is meaningful, and the examples are consistent.
lodicule decreased size: Lodicules are often described as small or minute.
flower bract filiform: Bracts can be filiform. Some examples describe an acumen (a tip), not the bract.
portion of secretory tissue low brightness: Dark glands: secretory tissue can be dark-coloured.
structure: 'Marginés' means having a distinct margin. PATO 'structure' is a generic attribute and the wrong reading.
glabrous: 'Becoming glabrous with age' is meaningful for surfaces and organs that bear hairs.
samara fruit scaly: Lepidote or scaly fruits are common and the examples are correct.
pappus falciform: The examples describe hooked, sigmoid or uncinate pappus bristles, not sickle-shaped (falciform) ones. The PATO term means something else.
length: Length measurements are meaningful for any measurable part.
triangular: Triangular is a normal shape for flat parts, and the examples fit.
subcircular: A lobe can be subcircular, as in the median lobe example.
sepal arrow-shaped: Sagittate sepals are meaningful. 'Sigmoïdes' is a mis-hit from the same stem.
leaf lamina attached to: 'Attached to' is a relation between two parts, not a quality of the lamina. It belongs in a relation or base-attachment rule.
shoot axis trichome pointed: Trichomes can be pointed, as in a unicellular pointed tip. Some examples are about auricles or the apex.
shoot system quadrangular: Shoots and twigs can be quadrangular.
shoot system robust: Robust shoots are a normal description.
shoot system straight: Shoots can be straight. One example is about prickles.
orbicular: Orbicular is a standard shape for flat parts.
bract prolate: 'Ellipsoid' is not 'prolate'. Bracts are flat, so ellipsoid maps to elliptic. This is a wrong reading.
inflorescence bract decreased length: Bracts are often shorter than the spikes or the peduncle. The comparison is to another part, so the length is relative.
inflorescence bract papyraceous: Papery or chartaceous bracts are common.
diameter: The ostiole has a diameter, and the examples are measurements.
shoot axis trichome sparse: Trichomes can be sparse. One example is about rhizome scales.
hydathode frequency: 'Hydathodes frequent' is about how frequent they are, so frequency fits.
vascular leaf spotted: Spotted or flecked leaves are a normal description.
length: Length measurements are meaningful for a measurable part.
stigma knobbled: A knobby stigma is meaningful and the examples are consistent.
sepal rose colour: Rose-coloured sepals are meaningful.
hemispheroid: Semiglobose is a hemispheroid shape and the examples fit.
flower nectary subulate: Nectary scales can be subulate. There is only one example.
caruncle fimbriated: A caruncle can be fimbriate.
arilloid lobed: Arilloids or pseudarils can be lobed, as the examples show.
awn spatial pattern: 'Solitary' is a count of awns per spikelet, not a spatial pattern. It belongs in a counted-parts rule.
length: The anther tube has a length, and the examples are measurements.
spore capsule calyptra glabrous: A hairless calyptra is a standard moss description.
hypanthium viscid: A viscid hypanthium is meaningful, and the examples are consistent.
lenticel protruding: Lenticels can be erumpent, meaning protruding.
cortex thickness: Cortex thickness is meaningful. The examples come from lichen text in Latin, so the part may be a lichen cortex rather than a plant cortex.
flower sericeous: Flowers or floral cups can be sericeous (silky) in many floras.
bud concealed: Buds can be hidden or concealed by leaves or petiole bases.
sepal pendent: Pendent sepals are meaningful. One example is about a spur.
bark colored: Bark can be coloured, and the examples are cinnamon-coloured bark. A specific colour term would be better if one exists.
capsule fruit pedicellate: A capsule can have a stalk (pedicel). The French example is about the pedicel itself, but the English ones are correct.
ascending: Lobes can point upward (ascending). I could not check what the FLOPO part class is, because its name is blank.
leaf lamina glutinous: Leaf blades can be sticky (glutinous).
lamina solid configuration: A blade can be solid, as opposed to hollow. There is only one example.
bulb increased size: A bulb can be large.
lenticel increased size: Lenticels can be large. The bare example 'enlarged' is uncertain.
bud sessile (sensu botany): Buds can be sessile (without a stalk).
inflorescence flexible: Inflorescences can be flexible. 'On lengths of flex' is a stray example.
perianth reflexed: A perianth or its lobes can be bent back (reflexed). Some examples are really about the lobes.
sepal terete: Sepals or sepal horns can be terete (round in cross-section).
root radiating: Roots can radiate from a point. This describes how they are arranged, but the pair is meaningful.
bracteole scaly: Bracteoles can be scaly, in the sense of scale-like.
leaf lamina tooth rough: 'Coarse teeth' means large or stout teeth, not a rough surface. The PATO term is read wrongly.
berry fruit fleshy: Berries can be fleshy or juicy.
raceme inflorescence branched: Racemes can be branched or unbranched.
exocarp inconspicuous: An exocarp can be inconspicuous. The examples are partly about cells, but the pair is fine.
involucral bract lance-ovate: Involucral bracts (phyllaries) can be lance-ovate.
perigynium prolate: 'Ellipsoid' is not 'prolate'. The ellipsoid term should be used instead.
perigynium ratio: A length-to-width ratio is a real measure of a perigynium.
achene fruit symmetrical: Achenes can be symmetric or asymmetric.
leaf lamina tooth cartilaginous: Teeth can be cartilaginous (firm and gristle-like).
perigynium present: A perigynium can be present or absent. The 'numerous' examples are really counts, so those are less certain.
smooth: The examples show a beak (or similar part) that can be smooth.
anther banded: Anthers can have stripes or bands.
nut fruit bent: 'Angled' means having angles or ridges, not bent. The PATO term is read wrongly.
leaf sheath auricle spiny: Auricles can be spiny or spinulose.
involucral bract straight: Involucral bracts or their tips can be straight.
involucral bract reflectivity: Bracts can be dull or shiny.
present: A mentum can be present or absent.
auriculate: The part can have ear-like lobes (auricles). The examples mix the quality with the presence of auricles.
branch aplastic: Branches can be suppressed or undeveloped.
style bristly: Styles can bear bristles.
leaf sinus increased depth: Leaf sinuses can be deep.
thorn retrorse: Thorns and prickles can point backward (retrorse).
perianth decreased width: A perianth can be narrow. Some examples are about the tube or wings, which are parts of the perianth.
corymb inflorescence amount: The examples count flowers per corymb, not corymbs. The counted thing is a different part, so the pair is a wrong reading.
hydathode sunken: Hydathodes can be sunken.
cauline leaf present: Cauline leaves can be present or absent. One example is unrelated.
tepal emarginate: Tepals can have a notched tip (emarginate).
areole bud subcircular: Areoles can be subcircular.
achene fruit characteristic: 'Characteristic' is a vague root term. The examples are specific qualities (glabrous, smooth) that need their own terms.
inflorescence bract entire: Bracts can have an entire (smooth, unbroken) margin.
truncated: An apex or lip can be truncate (cut off square).
seed coat undulate: A seed coat can have wavy margins or cell walls.
sorus spherical: Sori can be globose.
sorus straight: Sori can be straight or curved.
leaf lamina cylindrical: Leaf blades can be cylindrical.
gynoecium slender: A gynoecium or pistil can be slender. One example is about a stipe.
seed hexagonal: The examples describe seed pits or epidermal cells, not the seed. The hexagonal quality belongs to the cell or pit, so the part is wrong.
fruit sculpted surface: A fruit surface can be sculpted. One example is about the endocarp.
inflorescence laterally compressed: Inflorescences such as spikes can be laterally compressed.
decreased length: The part can be short. Some examples compare it with another organ, which is an extra relation.
stipule loose: Stipules, including the ocrea, can be loose.
shoot axis node amount: The examples count cones per node, not nodes. The counted part is the cone, so the pair is a wrong reading.

involucral bract cuspidate: Involucral bract apices are often cuspidate (Asteraceae). The 'broadly ovate, cuspidate' example fits.
ray flower elliptic: The example 'laminae elliptic' describes the lamina of the ray flower (ligule), not the whole flower. Elliptic belongs on the lamina or ligule part, so this pai
leaf lamina tooth lobed: 'Lobelike' means the tooth resembles a lobe. It is a comparison, not a lobed tooth. Lobed means divided into lobes, so the PATO term means something else here.
involucre sericeous: Involucres are often silky or sericeous (silky hairs). The examples are correct, including French 'soyeuses'.
bulb slender: A bulb can be slender (narrow and elongate). The examples are correct.
leaf margin hard: Indurate margins are hard in the botanical sense, so leaf margin and hard fit. The tooth examples are about teeth, not the margin, so a rule on teeth would be b
bulbous: A base (plant organ base) can be bulbous, meaning swollen. Examples including negations are handled by the negation rule.
sepal clasping: Sepals can clasp, for example in orchids where lateral sepals clasp the lip. The examples are correct.
protonema shape: The examples describe the leaf-like flaps and a mucronate point, not the shape of the protonema itself. The bearer is wrong for these statements. Protonema shap

perichaetal bract poorly differentiated: The examples are about the perichaetial leaves being little differentiated from vegetative leaves. This is a comparison between leaves, not a quality of the bra
perianth increased size: Perianths can be enlarged or large (for example in fruit). The examples are correct.
pappus characteristic: PATO_0000001 is the generic root term 'quality'. It is too general. The examples are about margin forms (entire or lacerate) and hairs (plumose), which belong t
palea firm: Paleas can be firm (texture). The examples are correct.
hypanthium inflated: Hypanthia can be inflated. The examples are correct.
capsule fruit curvature: Capsules can be curved. One example, 'à sutures déprimées' (depressed sutures), is a different quality and misannotated, but the pair itself is meaningful.
perigonial bract sharpness: Bract apices can be acute or apiculate. The quality describes the apex, so the pair fits when the apex is the bearer.
inflated: A spathe can be inflated, for example in Araceae. The examples are correct.
plant embryo increased size: Embryos can be large. The 'très larges cotylédons' example is about cotyledons, which is a different part, but the other examples fit.
flat: Fronds can be flat, as opposed to terete or folded. The examples are correct.
flower viscid: Flowers can be sticky or viscid (glandular hairs). The examples are correct.
stamen translucent: Filaments can be translucent. The examples are correct.
bracteole tapered: Bracteoles can be narrowed or tapering. The examples are correct.
root obconical: Roots, especially taproots, can be obconic. The examples are correct.
vascular bundle longitudinal orientation: Veins run longitudinally. The bearer 'vascular bundle' here stands for vein, and the examples are correct. A vein class would be better.
leaf lamina tangled: The examples say the surfaces are tangled, meaning hairs on the lamina. The tangled quality belongs to the indumentum (hairs), not the lamina.
inflorescence tangled: Inflorescences can be tangled (entangled branches). The examples fit.
paraphysis has fewer parts of type: 'Paraphyses few' is a count of paraphyses, with the paraphyses themselves as the thing counted. The bearer is the whole (for example the gametangium), so the pa
capsule fruit inflated: Capsules can be inflated. The examples are correct.
scale leaf ciliated: Scale leaves and cataphylls can have ciliate margins. The quality describes the margin, but the pair is meaningful.
scale leaf increased thickness: Scale leaves can be thick or thickened. The examples are correct.
pappus element present: 'Present' is not a useful quality here. The examples are counts or sizes of scales and hairs. A rule on counts and presence is needed.
stalk dilated: A stalk (stipe, rachis) can be dilated or expanded at the base or apex. The examples are correct.
plant ovary granular: The examples describe granular particles in the walls or appendages, not a granular ovary. The bearer is wrong.
petiole firm: Petioles can be firm. The examples are correct.
spadix inflorescence sharpness: A spadix apex can be acute or subacute. The quality describes the apex, but the pair is meaningful.
trichome shedability: Trichomes can be deciduous or persistent. The examples are correct.
inconspicuous: A rostellum can be obscure (inconspicuous) in orchids. The examples are correct.
sporangium base tapered: The sporangium base (neck, hypophysis) can taper. The examples are correct.
perianth keel-shaped: Perianths, especially of liverworts, can be keeled. The examples are correct.
capsule fruit slender: Capsules can be slender. The examples are correct.
trichome decreased strength: Hairs can be weak (soft, flimsy). The examples are correct.
perianth tapered: Perianths can be narrowed or tapered, for example at the base or the orifice. The examples are correct.
mesocarp coriaceous: Mesocarps can be leathery. The examples are correct.
involucral bract opaque: Involucral bracts can be opaque or translucent. The examples are correct.
trichome plumose: Trichomes can be plumose (feathery). The examples are correct, including French 'plumeuses'.
decreased thickness: Cupule (and its wall) can be thin. The examples are correct.
fruit fimbriated: Fruit parts such as the wall and the pappus can be fimbriate. One example describes scales, not the fruit, but the pair is meaningful.
obovate: A leaflet blade can be obovate. The examples are correct.
tepal bristly: Wrong reading. 'Bristlelike' describes the shape of the tepal (a perianth bristle), not a bristly hair covering. Bristle-shaped tepals need a shape term or a se
achene fruit umbonate: The apex of an achene can be umbonate.
higher order inflorescence axis recurved: Inflorescence branches can be recurved. The examples are correct.
sporophyll tapered: A sporophyll can taper to its apex or base.
sporophyll entire: A sporophyll margin can be entire.
leaf sheath auricle curved: A grass auricle can be curved or incurved.
sepal abaxial epidermis texture: The sepal epidermis can be papillate or papillose, which is a texture.
leaf lamina abaxial epidermis grooved: The abaxial surface of a lamina can be grooved or channelled.
leaf lamina lobe hastate: A lamina lobe can be hastate. The examples are correct.
cortex conspicuous: Wrong part. 'Conspicuous' describes the mucilage sacs or retort cells inside the cortex, not the cortex. Those cells need their own bearer.
cuspidate: A spathe apex can be cuspidate.
spadix inflorescence female: A spadix, or a portion of it, can be female (pistillate). The examples are correct.
involucre tapered: An involucre can taper to its base or apex.
achene fruit falciform: An achene can be falcate. The 'uncinate hairs' and 'hooked' examples are partly wrong readings (hairs, not the achene), but the pair is meaningful.
shoot axis internode winged: An internode can be winged.
leaf sheath reflectivity: A leaf sheath surface can be dull or shiny. The 'dull brown strigose' example is a colour reading and would need its own rule.
hemispheroid: An anther cap can be hemispherical. The examples are correct.
inconspicuous: Wrong reading. The examples describe the lobes or the boundary between epichile and hypochile, not the lip. The lip is normally the showy part.
samara fruit oblong: A samara can be oblong.
dentated: A pseudostaminode margin or apex can be dentate.
epicalyx decreased size: An epicalyx or its lobes can be small or minute.
color: Epicalyx segments can be coloured. The 'pilose' part of one example is a different quality, but the pair is fine.
root spheroid: Roots, especially tuberous ones, can be globose. The tuber reading is acceptable.
phyllome lamina lobe scalloped: A lobe margin can be crenate, which is scalloped.
costa glistening: A costa surface can be glossy or lustrous.
condensed: Wrong reading. 'Compressed' (flattened) is not 'condensed'. A compressed corolla lip needs a compressed or flattened term.
spheroid: A floral disc can be globose or cushion-shaped.
endocarp prolate: An endocarp can be ellipsoid. Prolate is the nearest PATO term.
oblong: Epicalyx segments can be oblong.
length: Disc glands have a length. The 'disk glands 0' example is noise.
inconspicuous: An indusium can be inconspicuous, obscured by the sporangia.
split: A tunic can split, for example along its veins.
pseudostem present: A pseudostem can be present or absent.
deciduous (generic): Perianth lobes can be deciduous.
staminode square: A staminode can be square.
elliptic: A spathe can be elliptic. The 'oval' example is acceptable.
smooth: A spadix appendix surface can be smooth.
shoot axis internode quadrangular: An internode can be four-angled (quadrangular).
bud lanate: A bud can be lanate (woolly).
pappus element slender: A pappus bristle or hair can be slender.
leaf midvein increased width: A midvein can be wide. Measured widths such as '0.25-0.5 mm wide' are a different pattern.
sorus depth: Wrong reading. 'Sori 1-2 mm from margin' is a distance between the sorus and the margin, not the depth of the sorus.
stalk up: A stalk or stipe can be directed upward.
vegetative bud ovate: A vegetative bud can be ovoid. This is a shape of the bud, but the closest PATO term here is ovate.
leaf lamina tooth decreased width: A leaf tooth can be narrow. Some examples are noisy.
lamina increased width: A lamina can be wide or broadened. Measured widths such as '4-5 mm wide' belong to the measurement pattern.
plant ovary glistening: An ovary surface can be shiny or glossy.
hastate: A pinna can be hastate.
ratio: An indusium can have a width-to-length ratio ('wider than long').
megasporangiate strobilus spheroid: A seed cone can be subglobose.
costa thickness: A costa can be thick, stout or slender, and can have a measured thickness.
petal granular: A petal surface can be granular. The 'glandular granulose' wording is a gland reading, but the texture is meaningful.
